quiz.title: Timed Mock Interview
quiz.description: Mixed-pattern questions across the core interview toolkit. Pick the best approach for each.

questions.prompt: Longest substring without repeating characters — the optimal approach is:
options: A sliding window with a last-seen index map
Sort the string, then scan for duplicates
Check every substring for uniqueness
Binary search on the answer length
questions.explanation: Expand the window's right edge; when a repeat appears, jump the left edge past the previous occurrence. O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet)) space.

questions.prompt: In a sorted array, find two numbers summing to a target in O(n) time and O(1) space:
options: Two pointers, one from each end
A hash map of complements
Two nested loops
Binary search for each element
questions.explanation: Move the left pointer right when the sum is too small and the right pointer left when it's too big. The hash-map answer is O(n) time but O(n) space.

questions.prompt: Worst-case comparisons to binary-search a sorted array of ~1,000,000 elements:
options: About 20
About 1,000
About 500,000
questions.explanation: Binary search is O(log₂ n). log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20, so at most ~20 comparisons.

questions.prompt: Maximum contiguous subarray sum in a single O(n) pass:
options: Kadane's algorithm
Sort then take the suffix
All-pairs prefix sums
Depth-first search
questions.explanation: Kadane keeps a running best-ending-here sum, resetting when it drops below zero. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.prompt: Detect a cycle in a linked list using O(1) extra space:
options: Floyd's fast & slow pointers
Store every visited node in a hash set
Reverse the list and compare
Sort the node addresses
questions.explanation: A slow pointer moving one step and a fast pointer moving two will meet inside any cycle. The hash-set approach works but costs O(n) space.

questions.prompt: Fewest coins to make an amount with unlimited denominations:
options: Dynamic programming (coin change)
Always take the largest coin (greedy)
Two pointers over sorted coins
Breadth-first search only
questions.explanation: Greedy fails for coin systems like {1, 3, 4} making 6. DP over subamounts guarantees the optimum in O(amount × coins).

quiz.title: Big Tech Set
quiz.description: Big-tech-style favourites, then real problems at scale — maps, feeds, sync, sharding. Pick the technique for each.

questions.prompt: Clone an undirected graph given a node reference:
options: BFS/DFS with an original→copy visited map
Topological sort then rebuild
Union-Find over the edges
Dijkstra from the given node
questions.explanation: Traverse once, creating a copy on first visit and wiring neighbours through the visited map to avoid infinite loops on cycles.

questions.prompt: Minimum window substring of S that contains all characters of T:
options: Sliding window with a need/have count
Sort both strings and diff them
Build a trie of T
Binary search the window size
questions.explanation: Grow the window until it covers T, then shrink from the left while it still covers T, tracking the smallest. O(|S| + |T|).

questions.prompt: Return the K points closest to the origin:
options: A size-K max-heap (or Quickselect)
Fully sort all points every time
Breadth-first search
Dynamic programming
questions.explanation: A size-K max-heap gives O(n log K); Quickselect gives O(n) average. A full sort is O(n log n) — more work than needed.

questions.prompt: Search for a target in a rotated sorted array in O(log n):
options: Modified binary search on the sorted half
Linear scan from the pivot
Hash every element first
Merge sort then binary search
questions.explanation: At each step one half is sorted; decide whether the target lies in it and recurse there, keeping O(log n).

questions.prompt: Container With Most Water — maximum area between two lines:
options: Two pointers moving the shorter wall inward
Check every pair of lines
Sort the heights first
A segment tree of heights
questions.explanation: Start at both ends; the area is bounded by the shorter wall, so moving it inward is the only way the area can grow. O(n).

questions.prompt: Scenario: a photo app gets millions of uploads a day, and exact duplicates of stored photos should not be saved twice.
options: Hash each file's bytes (e.g. SHA-256) and look the digest up in a hash set
Compare each new photo byte by byte with every stored photo
Compare file names
Sort all photos by size every night and compare neighbours
questions.explanation: Solve: digest = sha256(bytes); if digest is already stored, point the upload at the existing file, otherwise store it and the digest. One hash per upload and an O(1) average lookup, whatever the library size. File names say nothing about content. Near-duplicates (resized, re-encoded) need a perceptual hash instead — worth mentioning as a follow-up.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a maps app needs the fastest driving route between two intersections. Roads have travel times.
options: Dijkstra on travel time — in practice A* with a straight-line-distance heuristic
BFS, counting roads instead of time
DFS, returning the first route that reaches the destination
Floyd-Warshall over the whole country on every request
questions.explanation: Solve: intersections are nodes and roads are weighted edges, so it is weighted shortest path. Travel times are never negative, so Dijkstra is correct; A* expands far fewer nodes by preferring ones closer to the goal (distance ÷ top speed never overestimates). BFS minimises the number of roads, not time. Floyd-Warshall is O(V³) on millions of nodes.

questions.prompt: Scenario: suggest "People you may know" — people the user is not friends with, ranked by mutual friends.
options: Go two hops out from the user, count how often each second-hop person appears, then take the top k
Suggest random users
Run a DFS over the whole social graph
Compute all-pairs shortest paths
questions.explanation: Solve: for each friend f, for each friend g of f: if g is not the user and not already a friend, count[g]++. count[g] is exactly the number of mutual friends. Then a size-k heap picks the best. Only two levels are touched, which is the whole trick — the full graph has billions of edges.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a ride-hailing app must find the nearest available drivers to a rider, among millions of moving drivers.
options: A spatial index — geohash grid cells or a k-d tree — searching the rider's cell and its neighbours
Scan every driver and compute each distance
Sort drivers by latitude only
A hash map keyed by driver id
questions.explanation: Solve: bucket drivers by grid cell (geohash) and update a driver's cell as they move. For a rider, check their cell and the 8 around it, widening the ring if too few drivers are found. That touches a few hundred drivers, not millions. Sorting by latitude alone ignores longitude; an id map cannot answer anything about location.

figure.caption: City grid: R = rider, D = free driver

questions.prompt: Scenario: a cloud drive syncs a 2 GB file after a small edit near its start. How do you upload only what changed?
options: Split it into content-defined chunks with a rolling hash, hash each chunk, and upload only unknown hashes
Upload the whole file every time
Split into fixed 4 MB blocks and compare their hashes
Compare the file size and modification time
questions.explanation: Solve: slide a rolling hash over the bytes and cut a chunk wherever it matches a pattern (e.g. its low 13 bits are 0). Boundaries follow the content, so an insertion only changes the chunks around it. With fixed blocks, one inserted byte shifts every later block and all of them look changed. Size and time only say that something changed, not what.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a spreadsheet app must stop the user creating a circular reference, such as A1 = B1 + 1 and B1 = A1 × 2.
options: DFS over formula references with three states (unvisited, in progress, done) — reaching an in-progress cell is a cycle
Count how many formulas reference each cell
BFS that keeps no visited state
Union-find over the references
questions.explanation: Solve: cells are nodes and "A1 uses B1" is a directed edge. DFS from the edited cell; meeting a cell that is still on the current path means a loop. The same graph in topological order is also the order to recalculate cells in. Union-find ignores direction, so it would flag harmless diamonds (two cells both using a third).

figure.caption: Formula references (A → B: A uses B)

questions.prompt: Scenario: find the 1,000 most frequent search queries of the day from 10 billion log lines spread across 1,000 machines.
options: Shard by hash(query) so every copy of a query is counted on one machine, keep a size-1,000 heap per shard, then merge the heaps
Copy every log to one machine and sort it
Have each machine send only its local top 1,000
Take a random sample of 1,000 queries
questions.explanation: Solve: map — every machine emits (query, count) from a local hash map; shuffle — route by hash(query), so each query's total lands in exactly one place; reduce — each shard keeps its own top 1,000 in a min-heap; finally merge those candidate lists. Local top lists are wrong: a query that is 1,001st on every machine can be first overall.

questions.prompt: Scenario: design the code generator for a URL shortener that will store billions of links.
options: Encode a unique increasing id in base 62 — 7 characters give 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 × 10¹² codes
Use the first 7 characters of the long URL
Pick a random 3-letter code
Use the full 32-character MD5 of the URL
questions.explanation: Solve: take an id from a counter (hand out ranges to each server so they never clash), then write it in base 62 with 0-9, a-z and A-Z. Codes are unique by construction, with no collision check. URL prefixes collide constantly (every "https:/"); 3 letters give only 17,576 codes; a full MD5 is not short.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a cache is spread over n servers. When a server is added, as few keys as possible should move.
options: Consistent hashing on a ring, with virtual nodes — only about 1/n of the keys move
Put each key on server hash(key) % n
Assign keys to servers round-robin
Pick a random server on every request
questions.explanation: Solve: hash servers and keys onto the same ring; a key belongs to the first server clockwise from it. A new server only takes keys from its neighbour's arc. With hash % n, changing n remaps almost every key and the whole cache goes cold at once. Virtual nodes (many ring points per server) even out the load.

figure.caption: Hash ring: servers S and keys k

questions.prompt: Scenario: a calendar app finds the first free 30-minute slot for 5 people, given each person's busy intervals.
options: Merge everyone's busy intervals (sorted by start), then return the first gap of at least 30 minutes
Pick a random time and check it
Intersect only the first two people's calendars
Take the first person's earliest free slot
questions.explanation: Solve: put all busy intervals into one list, sort by start, and merge any that overlap. The gaps between merged blocks (and before the first one, from the start of the working day) are when everyone is free, so scan for one ≥ 30 minutes. O(N log N) for N intervals. Checking only two people ignores the other three.

quiz.title: Startup Set
quiz.description: Practical questions in the style of fast-moving product companies, then real product problems to solve.

questions.prompt: Design a cache with O(1) get and put that evicts the least-recently-used entry:
options: Hash map + doubly linked list
A sorted array of timestamps
A single hash map with periodic sweeps
A min-heap keyed by access time
questions.explanation: The map gives O(1) lookup; the doubly linked list moves a touched node to the front and drops the tail on eviction, both O(1).

questions.prompt: Deduplicate a stream of events while preserving first-seen order:
options: A hash set for membership plus a list for order
Sort the stream and remove neighbours
Nested loops comparing every pair
A balanced BST of all events
questions.explanation: The set answers 'seen before?' in O(1); append to the ordered list only on first sight. O(n) time.

questions.prompt: Maintain the Kth-largest value in a growing stream:
options: A size-K min-heap
Re-sort the whole stream on each insert
A size-K max-heap
A hash map of counts
questions.explanation: Keep only K elements; the heap root is the Kth largest. Push/pop is O(log K). A max-heap would need K pops to answer.

questions.prompt: Serve type-ahead suggestions for every prefix of a search box, over a fixed vocabulary:
options: A trie, with the top completions cached at each node
A hash set of the whole vocabulary
Binary search the sorted vocabulary on each keystroke
A max-heap keyed by word frequency
questions.explanation: A hash set answers 'is this a word?' but cannot enumerate by prefix. Walking the trie costs O(prefix length), and caching each node's best completions makes the suggestion list a single read.

questions.prompt: Maximum profit from a single buy then sell over a price series:
options: One pass tracking the minimum price so far
Check every buy/sell pair
Sort the prices ascending
Binary search the best day
questions.explanation: Track the lowest price seen and the best profit against it in a single O(n) sweep — the same running-best idea as Kadane.

questions.prompt: Scenario: roll a new checkout out to 10% of users. Each user must see the same version on every visit and every device.
options: Hash the user id into buckets 0–99 and enable it when the bucket is below 10
Flip a random coin on every request
Enable it for the first 10% of users by signup date
Store a random flag in each browser session
questions.explanation: Solve: bucket = hash(featureName + userId) % 100; enabled = bucket < 10. It is deterministic, so it is stable across sessions and devices with nothing stored, and ramping to 50% is a config change. Adding the feature name keeps the same users from being first in every experiment. Per-request coins flicker; signup date gives a biased group (only old users).

questions.prompt: Scenario: a referral programme pays per signup. Fraudsters create many accounts that share phones or payment cards. Group the accounts that belong together.
options: Union-find: union any two accounts that share a device, card or phone number; each set is one group
Flag accounts created on the same day
Sort accounts by name and compare neighbours
Run a BFS from each account separately, with no shared state
questions.explanation: Solve: map each device/card/phone → the first account seen with it; when another account shows the same one, union them. Links chain transitively — A shares a phone with B, B a card with C — so one set can be a whole ring. Near O(1) per link, and it works as events stream in.

figure.caption: Accounts linked by the phone or card they used

questions.prompt: Scenario: a feed API pages with OFFSET/LIMIT, and users see duplicates on page 2 when new posts arrive. The fix:
options: Cursor pagination: return posts older than the last seen (timestamp, id) pair
Increase the page size
Load the whole feed into the app once
Cache page 1 for an hour
questions.explanation: Solve: page 1 returns a cursor = (createdAt, id) of its last post; page 2 asks for WHERE (createdAt, id) < cursor ORDER BY createdAt DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20. New posts land above the cursor, so nothing shifts. The id breaks timestamp ties. It is also faster: an index seek instead of skipping OFFSET rows.

questions.prompt: Scenario: generate 1,000,000 single-use coupon codes that customers cannot guess.
options: Random codes from a large alphabet (e.g. 10 base-32 characters ≈ 10¹⁵ options), checked against a set of issued codes
Sequential numbers such as SAVE000001
The first 4 characters of a hash of the customer's email
One shared code for everyone
questions.explanation: Solve: draw each code from a cryptographically secure random source; re-draw on the rare collision with the issued set. With 10¹⁵ possibilities and 10⁶ codes, a guess succeeds about once in a billion tries — add rate limiting to redemption. Sequential codes can be enumerated; 4 hex characters are only 65,536 options.

questions.prompt: Scenario: search-as-you-type sends a request on every keystroke, and the search servers are overloaded. The first fix:
options: Debounce: send only after the user pauses for about 300 ms, and cancel requests that are out of date
Add more servers
Send a request only for every tenth keystroke
Search only after the user presses Enter
questions.explanation: Solve: restart a 300 ms timer on each keystroke and fire only when it expires, so typing "android" sends 1 request instead of 7. Cancel the in-flight request when a newer one starts, so a slow old response cannot overwrite a newer one. More servers pay for waste; every-tenth-keystroke searches for half-typed words.

questions.prompt: Scenario: an expense-splitting app must settle a group's debts with as few payments as possible.
options: Net each person's balance, then match debtors against creditors — at most n − 1 payments
Replay every original IOU as its own payment
Everyone pays whoever paid the most
Split every bill equally again
questions.explanation: Solve: balance = paid − owed for each person; the IOUs themselves no longer matter. Repeatedly let the biggest debtor pay the biggest creditor min(debt, credit); each payment clears at least one person, so n people need at most n − 1. The true minimum (finding subgroups that net to zero) is NP-hard — worth saying out loud.

figure.caption: Who owes whom (after a weekend trip)

questions.prompt: Scenario: a CSV import of 1,000,000 customer rows has repeated emails in different casing. Keep only the latest row per customer.
options: One pass with a map from normalised email (trimmed, lowercased) to the latest row
Compare every row with every other row
Remove rows whose email appears exactly twice
Sort by email as typed and drop neighbours
questions.explanation: Solve: key = email.trim().lowercase(); if the row is newer than map[key], replace it. O(n) time. Without normalising, "Ann@x.com" and "ann@x.com " count as different people — sorting the raw values misses them. Pairwise comparison is 10¹² operations.

questions.prompt: Scenario: the app lets users schedule emails for any future time. Send each one on time.
options: A min-heap (priority queue) keyed by send time; the worker sleeps until the top one is due
Scan every scheduled email once a second
A sorted list with a linear scan on every insert
One sleeping timer thread per email
questions.explanation: Solve: insert is O(log n). The worker peeks at the top: if it is due, pop and send; otherwise sleep until its time, or until a new, earlier email arrives. Scanning is O(n) every second; a thread per email collapses at a million. Store the jobs durably too, so a restart does not lose them.

questions.prompt: Scenario: products are ranked by star rating. A product with a single 5-star review beats one with 4.8 from 2,000 reviews. The fix:
options: Rank by the lower bound of a confidence interval (e.g. the Wilson score), not the raw average
Rank by the raw average rating
Rank by the number of reviews only
Hide every product with fewer than 1,000 reviews
questions.explanation: Solve: the lower bound asks "how good is this product at least, given how few reviews there are?" One 5-star review gives a wide interval and a low bound; 2,000 reviews at 4.8 give a tight, high one. Review count alone ignores quality, and a hard cutoff hides every new product.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a user edits the same note on a phone and a laptop. The later save silently overwrites the other one. The fix:
options: Optimistic locking: each save sends the version it was based on; reject a stale version and ask to merge
Last write wins
Lock the note for 24 hours after it is opened
Save only from whichever device was used most recently
questions.explanation: Solve: store a version number with the note. UPDATE … SET body = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?; if zero rows change, someone else saved first, so show both versions to merge. Nothing is held while the user is typing, unlike a lock, and no edit is lost, unlike last-write-wins.

quiz.title: Finance / Trading Set
quiz.description: Latency- and math-heavy questions in the flavour of quant and trading interviews, then desk scenarios to solve.

questions.prompt: Report the running median of a live price stream:
options: Two heaps — a max-heap of the low half, a min-heap of the high half
Re-sort the stream on every tick
A single min-heap
A hash map of price counts
questions.explanation: Balance the two heaps so their tops straddle the median; each insert is O(log n) and the median is O(1).

questions.prompt: Report the highest price in the trailing k ticks, updated on every tick:
options: A monotonic deque of indices, dropping any tick a newer higher one dominates
A max-heap of the last k prices
Rescan the k-tick window on each tick
A running maximum that resets when the window slides
questions.explanation: Each index is pushed and popped once, so the whole stream costs O(n) with the answer at the deque's front. A heap is O(n log k) and needs lazy deletion; a running max cannot recover when the tick holding the maximum leaves the window.

questions.prompt: Compute a^n for a large integer n as fast as possible:
options: Exponentiation by squaring — O(log n)
Multiply a by itself n times — O(n)
Take the logarithm and exponentiate
A lookup table of all powers
questions.explanation: Square the base and halve the exponent each step: a^n = (a^(n/2))². O(log n) multiplications.

questions.prompt: Count the number of ways to make an amount from unlimited denominations:
options: DP iterating coins in the outer loop
Greedy — always take the largest coin
Two pointers over sorted coins
Breadth-first search
questions.explanation: Looping coins outer and amounts inner counts combinations without double-counting orderings. Greedy answers the min-coins variant, not the count.

questions.prompt: Find where a new price would be inserted into a sorted order book, in O(log n):
options: Binary search for the lower bound
Linear scan from the best bid
Hash the price levels
Insertion sort the new price
questions.explanation: Lower-bound binary search returns the first index whose value is ≥ the target — the insertion point — in O(log n).

questions.prompt: Scenario: design a matching engine's order book — add orders, cancel by id, and always know the best bid and best ask.
options: Per side, a sorted map of price → FIFO queue of orders, plus a map of order id → order for O(1) cancels
One unsorted list of all orders, scanned for every trade
A single hash map from price to quantity
Re-sort every order on each tick
questions.explanation: Solve: bids sorted high to low, asks low to high, so each best price is the first entry. Within a price level a FIFO queue gives time priority — first in, first filled. The id map finds an order for cancellation without searching its level. Adding a new price level is O(log levels); everything else is O(1).

questions.prompt: Scenario: show the volume-weighted average price (VWAP) of the last 5 minutes, updated on every trade.
options: A queue of recent trades with running sums of price × volume and of volume; evict trades older than 5 minutes
Recompute from every trade of the day on each tick
Average the prices, ignoring volume
Keep a max-heap of prices
questions.explanation: Solve: on each trade push it and add p·v to S and v to V; pop from the front while the oldest trade is over 5 minutes old, subtracting it. VWAP = S / V. Each trade enters and leaves once — O(1) amortised. A plain average lets a 1-share trade count as much as a 100,000-share block.

questions.prompt: Scenario: given exchange rates between currencies, detect an arbitrage loop (trade round a cycle and end with more than you started).
options: Take −log of every rate; a negative cycle (found with Bellman-Ford) is an arbitrage loop
Dijkstra on the raw rates
Always take the best rate out of each currency
Topologically sort the currencies
questions.explanation: Solve: a loop is profitable when r₁·r₂·…·rₖ > 1. Taking logs turns the product into a sum; negating turns "> 0" into "< 0". So arbitrage is exactly a negative cycle, which Bellman-Ford detects on its V-th round. Dijkstra breaks on negative edges; currency graphs are full of cycles, so they have no topological order.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a payments service stores account balances. Which type should hold money?
options: Integer minor units (cents) or a decimal type — never binary floating point
A double — 64 bits is plenty of precision
A float, rounded to 2 places after each operation
A string, parsed whenever it is needed
questions.explanation: Solve: 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.30000000000000004, and those errors add up across millions of transactions. Store 1,050 cents as a Long, or use BigDecimal with an explicit rounding mode. Rounding floats after each step still accumulates error and breaks exact equality checks.

questions.prompt: Scenario: report a fund's maximum drawdown — the largest fall from a peak to a later low — over a price history.
options: One pass tracking the running peak and the largest (peak − price) / peak
The overall maximum minus the overall minimum
Sort the prices and compare the ends
The largest single-day fall
questions.explanation: Solve: peak = max(peak, p); dd = max(dd, (peak − p) / peak). O(n), O(1). The drop must come after the peak, so the global max minus min is wrong when the minimum comes first. Several small daily falls can add up to a drawdown far larger than any single day.

questions.prompt: Scenario: users have set 1,000,000 price alerts on a stock. Each tick, fire every alert the price just crossed.
options: Keep alert thresholds sorted; on each move, binary search the range between the old and new price and fire those
Check every alert on every tick
A hash map keyed by the exact alert price
Check all alerts once at market close
questions.explanation: Solve: when the price moves from 101.20 to 101.55, only thresholds in (101.20, 101.55] were crossed. Two binary searches find that slice in O(log n) plus the alerts fired. Checking all of them is 10⁶ comparisons per tick. An exact-price map misses crossings, because the price jumps past most values without ever equalling them.

questions.prompt: Scenario: you price an option by Monte Carlo simulation and want to halve the estimate's standard error. How many more paths do you need?
options: 4× as many — the error shrinks like 1 / √N
2× as many — the error shrinks like 1 / N
The same number, run twice
Any number — the error does not depend on N
questions.explanation: Solve: standard error = σ / √N, so halving it needs √N to double, which means N × 4. Ten times more precision costs 100 times more paths. That is why variance-reduction tricks (antithetic variates, control variates) matter: they shrink σ instead of growing N.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a latency-critical pricing loop walks the same data millions of times per second. Why is an array usually faster than a linked list here?
options: Contiguous memory is cache-friendly — the CPU prefetches the next elements; list nodes are scattered
Arrays have better Big-O for sequential iteration
Linked lists use more CPU instructions per element
Arrays skip the garbage collector entirely
questions.explanation: Solve: both are O(n) to walk, so Big-O cannot explain it. A cache miss costs roughly 100 ns against about 1 ns for a hit; an array brings 8–16 values in per cache line, while each list node can be a fresh miss. In hot loops, memory layout outweighs the instruction count.

questions.prompt: Brainteaser: roll a fair die and receive the number shown. You may re-roll once and must keep the second roll. What is the expected payout with the best strategy?
options: 4.25 — re-roll on 1, 2 or 3
3.5 — the plain average of a die
4.5 — re-roll on anything below 6
5 — keep only 4, 5 or 6
questions.explanation: Solve: a re-roll is worth 3.5, so keep any first roll above 3.5. P(keep) = 1/2 with an average of 5; otherwise re-roll for 3.5. EV = ½ · 5 + ½ · 3.5 = 4.25. Re-rolling a 4 or 5 swaps a sure 4 or 5 for an average of 3.5, which lowers the payout.

questions.prompt: Scenario: sample one trade at random for an audit, with each trade's chance proportional to its volume.
options: Prefix sums of the volumes, then draw r in [0, total) and binary search for the first prefix above r
Pick a trade uniformly at random
Always pick the largest trade
Repeat each trade's id once per share, then pick from that list
questions.explanation: Solve: prefix = [v₁, v₁ + v₂, …]; r = random(0, total); return the first index with prefix[i] > r. O(n) setup and O(log n) per draw. Repeating ids per share is also correct, but a 1,000,000-share trade becomes a million entries.

quiz.title: ML Engineer Set
quiz.description: ML-engineer screen questions — modelling plus production reality.

questions.prompt: A fraud model scores 99.5% accuracy on data where 0.5% of transactions are fraud. The right reaction is:
options: Accuracy is meaningless here — report precision, recall and PR-AUC
Ship it; the accuracy is excellent
Increase the training set size
Switch to mean squared error
questions.explanation: Predicting 'not fraud' always scores 99.5%. Under heavy imbalance the minority class needs precision/recall, and PR-AUC discriminates better than ROC-AUC.

questions.prompt: Offline AUC improved but the online click-through rate dropped after rollout. The first thing to check is:
options: Training/serving skew and leakage in the offline evaluation
Whether the learning rate was too high
The number of hidden layers
Whether the GPU was saturated
questions.explanation: The classic causes are features computed differently online than offline, and an offline split that leaked future information. Both inflate offline scores without any real gain.

questions.prompt: For a time-series forecasting model, the correct validation split is:
options: Chronological — train on the past, validate on the future
Random k-fold across all rows
Stratified by the target value
Leave-one-out over the whole series
questions.explanation: Random folds let the model see future points while predicting the past — leakage that random splits hide. Rolling-origin (walk-forward) validation mirrors deployment.

questions.prompt: Gradient-boosted trees usually beat a deep net on mid-size tabular data because they:
options: Handle mixed feature types and non-linear splits with little tuning or data
Have more parameters
Train on GPUs more efficiently
Are immune to overfitting
questions.explanation: Boosted trees are scale-invariant, need no encoding of monotone relationships and fit sharp thresholds from thousands of rows — where a net would need far more data and tuning.

questions.prompt: Serving a large model under a tight latency budget most directly calls for:
options: Quantisation or distillation into a smaller student model
A larger batch size at training time
More dropout
Switching the optimiser to Adam
questions.explanation: Both shrink inference cost: quantisation lowers numeric precision, distillation trains a small model on the large one's outputs. Caching and batching help too — training-time knobs do not.

questions.prompt: Input feature distributions shifted but labels have not arrived yet. This is:
options: Data drift — detectable without labels, and an early warning for accuracy loss
Concept drift, which needs no monitoring
Overfitting
A leakage bug
questions.explanation: Data drift is a change in P(x); concept drift is a change in P(y|x) and needs labels to see. Watching inputs and prediction distributions buys warning time while labels lag.

quiz.title: Arrays & Strings
quiz.description: Indexing, shifting, windows and in-place edits.

questions.prompt: Inserting at the front of an array of n elements costs:
options: O(n) — every element shifts one slot right
O(1) — arrays grow at the front
O(log n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Arrays are contiguous, so making room at index 0 shifts all n elements. Only appending at the tail is O(1) amortized.

questions.prompt: A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. The amortized cost of one append is:
options: O(n) — every append copies
O(log n)
O(n²) across n appends
questions.explanation: Doubling makes copies rare: n appends cost n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n total work, so each append averages O(1).

questions.prompt: Which problem is NOT a natural fit for a sliding window?
options: Longest subsequence (non-contiguous) with a property
Longest substring without repeating characters
Maximum sum subarray of fixed size k
Smallest subarray with sum ≥ target, all values positive
questions.explanation: A window is always contiguous. Subsequences allow gaps, so they need DP or another technique.

questions.prompt: To answer many range-sum queries on a fixed array in O(1) each, precompute:
options: Prefix sums
A sorted copy
A hash map of every subarray
A balanced BST
questions.explanation: With prefix[i] holding the sum of the first i elements, sum(l..r) = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l].

questions.prompt: Reversing a string in place with two pointers uses how much extra space?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n) only for odd lengths
questions.explanation: Swapping from both ends inward needs only the two indices and one temporary — no second buffer.

questions.prompt: Why does a sliding window fail for "count subarrays summing to k" when negatives are allowed?
options: The running sum is no longer monotone, so shrinking cannot be decided
Windows cannot hold negative numbers
The window would exceed the array bounds
It works fine — negatives change nothing
questions.explanation: Shrinking a window assumes removing an element lowers the sum. With negatives it can raise it, so prefix sums with a hash map are used instead.

questions.prompt: An array holds each of 1..n once except that one value is missing and one is duplicated. Finding both in O(n) time and O(1) extra space uses:
options: Cyclic sort — swap each value to index value − 1, then scan for the mismatch
A hash set of everything seen so far
Sorting the array, then scanning for the gap
Binary search over the value range
questions.explanation: Because the values are exactly the index range, the array can be its own hash table: keep swapping until each slot holds its own value. The one index still holding the wrong value names both the duplicate and the missing number. The hash set is O(n) space and sorting is O(n log n).

quiz.title: Linked Lists
quiz.description: Pointer rewiring, cycles and traversal costs.

questions.prompt: Accessing the kth element of a singly linked list costs:
options: O(k) — you must walk from the head
O(1) — same as an array
O(log k)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Nodes are scattered in memory with no index arithmetic, so position is only reachable by traversal.

questions.prompt: Detecting a cycle in O(1) extra space uses:
options: Floyd's fast and slow pointers
A visited hash set
Sorting the nodes
Binary search on node index
questions.explanation: Inside a cycle the gap between a 1-step and a 2-step pointer closes by one per iteration, so they must meet. A hash set works but costs O(n) space.

questions.prompt: When reversing a list iteratively, the classic bug is:
options: Overwriting cur.next before saving it, losing the rest of the list
Starting prev at the head instead of null
Returning cur instead of prev
Using a while loop rather than recursion
questions.explanation: cur.next is the only reference to the remainder. Save it in a local before flipping the pointer.

questions.prompt: A dummy head node is used mainly to:
options: Remove the special case of modifying the real head
Speed up traversal
Store the list length
Allow random access
questions.explanation: With a node in front of the head, insertion and deletion at position 0 use the same code as anywhere else.

questions.prompt: Deleting a known node from a doubly linked list, given a reference to it, costs:
options: O(n) — you must find its predecessor
O(log n)
O(n) only for the tail
questions.explanation: The back-pointer gives the predecessor directly. In a singly linked list the same operation is O(n) because the predecessor must be found.

questions.prompt: After fast and slow meet inside a cycle, moving one pointer back to the head and advancing both by one lands them at:
options: The node where the cycle begins
The meeting point again
The list's midpoint
The last node before the cycle closes
questions.explanation: Slow travelled F + a and fast twice that, giving F = kL - a. So the distance head→entry equals meeting-point→entry.

quiz.title: Stacks & Queues
quiz.description: LIFO, FIFO, monotonic stacks and deques.

questions.prompt: Checking balanced brackets requires a stack because:
options: The next bracket that must close is always the most recently opened one
Counting brackets is impossible without one
Stacks sort the brackets
It gives O(1) random access
questions.explanation: Counting alone accepts "([)]". LIFO order is exactly what nesting demands.

questions.prompt: A monotonic decreasing stack is the standard tool for:
options: Next greater element
Sorting in O(n)
Cycle detection
Shortest paths
questions.explanation: Indices waiting for a larger value stay on the stack in decreasing order; one bigger arrival resolves all of them at once.

questions.prompt: BFS uses a queue rather than a stack because:
options: FIFO order visits all nodes at distance d before any at d + 1
Queues are faster than stacks
A stack cannot store graph nodes
Queues remove duplicates automatically
questions.explanation: Swapping in a stack turns the same code into DFS — the container choice *is* the traversal order.

questions.prompt: Implementing a queue with two stacks gives amortized dequeue cost of:
options: O(n) every time
O(log n)
O(n) only when empty
questions.explanation: Elements move from the in-stack to the out-stack at most once each, so the occasional O(n) transfer averages to O(1).

questions.prompt: A circular buffer queue avoids which cost of a naive array queue?
options: Shifting every element left after each dequeue
Allocating memory at all
Comparisons during enqueue
Recursion depth
questions.explanation: Advancing a head index modulo capacity makes dequeue O(1) instead of O(n).

questions.prompt: Supporting getMin() in O(1) alongside push and pop requires:
options: A parallel stack of the minimum at each depth
Sorting on every push
A single min variable
A binary search tree
questions.explanation: A single variable cannot be restored after popping the current minimum. Storing the minimum per depth restores it for free.

quiz.title: Trees & BST
quiz.description: Traversal orders, balance and the BST invariant.

questions.prompt: In-order traversal of a valid BST produces values in:
options: Ascending sorted order
Level order
Insertion order
Descending order
questions.explanation: Left subtree, node, right subtree — with the BST invariant this visits every value in ascending order.

questions.prompt: Search in a BST degrades from O(log n) to O(n) when:
options: The tree is degenerate — essentially a linked list
The tree is perfectly balanced
Values are duplicated
The tree stores strings
questions.explanation: Inserting sorted data produces a single chain, so height becomes n. Self-balancing trees exist to prevent this.

questions.prompt: Validating a BST by checking only node.left < node < node.right is wrong because:
options: Every node is also bounded by all its ancestors
Left and right must be compared to each other
It ignores null children
It is O(n²)
questions.explanation: A node deep in a right subtree must exceed the ancestor it turned right from. Thread a (low, high) range down the recursion.

questions.prompt: Level-order traversal needs which structure?
options: A queue
A stack
A min-heap
A hash map
questions.explanation: Children are enqueued behind the current level, so a level finishes before the next begins. Snapshot the queue size to separate levels.

questions.prompt: Recursive DFS on a tree of height h uses how much stack space?
options: O(h), which is O(n) for a degenerate tree
O(1) always
O(n) always
O(log n) always
questions.explanation: Only the current root-to-node path is on the stack. Balanced means O(log n); a chain means O(n) and risks overflow.

questions.prompt: A trie beats a hash set for which task?
options: Finding all stored words with a given prefix
Testing exact membership fastest
Sorting numbers
Detecting cycles
questions.explanation: A hash destroys prefix structure. A trie walks the prefix path once and enumerates the subtree below it.

quiz.title: Graphs
quiz.description: Representations, BFS/DFS and shortest paths.

questions.prompt: For a sparse graph, an adjacency list beats an adjacency matrix mainly in:
options: Space — O(V + E) instead of O(V²)
Edge-existence lookup time
Simplicity of code
Cache locality
questions.explanation: A matrix stores a slot per node pair regardless of edges. The matrix does win on O(1) edge lookup.

questions.prompt: Shortest path in an UNWEIGHTED graph is found by:
options: BFS
DFS
Dijkstra only
Topological sort
questions.explanation: BFS expands by distance, so the first time it reaches a node is via a minimum-edge path. Dijkstra works but adds needless heap overhead.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm fails when the graph has:
options: Negative edge weights
Cycles
More than 1000 nodes
Disconnected components
questions.explanation: It finalises a node on first extraction, which a later negative edge could undercut. Bellman-Ford handles negatives.

questions.prompt: Kahn's algorithm reports a cycle when:
options: Fewer nodes are output than the graph contains
The queue starts empty
Any node has in-degree above one
The graph is disconnected
questions.explanation: Nodes inside a cycle never reach in-degree zero, so they never enter the queue and the count falls short.

questions.prompt: Counting connected components in a grid is usually done with:
options: Flood fill via DFS/BFS, or union-find
Binary search
A monotonic stack
Topological sort
questions.explanation: Each unvisited land cell starts one traversal that consumes its whole component. Union-find is the alternative when edges stream in.

questions.prompt: Detecting a cycle in an UNDIRECTED graph with DFS requires:
options: Ignoring the edge back to the parent
Marking every node visited twice
Sorting the adjacency list
A priority queue
questions.explanation: Every undirected edge appears in both directions, so without skipping the parent every edge looks like a 2-cycle.

quiz.title: Sorting & Searching
quiz.description: Stability, pivots and logarithmic search.

questions.prompt: A stable sort guarantees that:
options: Equal elements keep their original relative order
It never exceeds O(n log n)
It uses O(1) space
It works on linked lists only
questions.explanation: Stability matters when sorting by a second key after a first. Merge sort is stable; quicksort and heapsort are not.

questions.prompt: Quicksort degrades to O(n²) when:
options: Pivots repeatedly split the array very unevenly
The array is large
The array contains negatives
Recursion is replaced by iteration
questions.explanation: A worst-case pivot peels one element per level, giving n levels of O(n) work. Randomised or median-of-three pivots avoid it.

questions.prompt: Counting sort can beat O(n log n) because it:
options: Does not compare elements — it indexes by value
Uses a better comparison order
Runs in parallel
Sorts in place
questions.explanation: The Ω(n log n) bound applies only to comparison sorts. Counting sort is O(n + k) but needs a bounded value range.

questions.prompt: Computing mid as (lo + hi) / 2 rather than lo + (hi - lo) / 2 risks:
options: Integer overflow on large bounds
An infinite loop
Skipping the first element
Nothing — they are identical
questions.explanation: lo + hi can exceed Int.MAX_VALUE and wrap negative. The subtraction form never overflows.

questions.prompt: "Binary searching the answer" is valid when the feasibility test is:
options: Monotone — once true, true for every larger candidate
Constant time
Randomised
Applied to a sorted array only
questions.explanation: Monotonicity gives the sorted structure to halve. That is why minimum-eating-speed and capacity problems yield to it.

questions.prompt: Finding the kth largest element in O(n) average time uses:
options: Quickselect
Merge sort then index
A full heapsort
Binary search on the array
questions.explanation: Quickselect recurses into only the side holding k, giving n + n/2 + n/4 … = O(n) average. A size-k heap is O(n log k).

quiz.title: Hashing & Heaps
quiz.description: Collisions, load factor and priority queues.

questions.prompt: Hash map lookup is O(1) on average but O(n) in the worst case because:
options: All keys can collide into one bucket
Resizing happens on every insert
Hashing itself is O(n)
Keys must be sorted first
questions.explanation: A degenerate hash turns every lookup into a scan of one long chain. Tree-ified buckets soften this to O(log n).

questions.prompt: Raising a hash table's load factor threshold trades:
options: Less memory for more collisions
More memory for more collisions
Speed for correctness
Nothing measurable
questions.explanation: A fuller table resizes less often but packs more keys per bucket, lengthening probe and chain walks.

questions.prompt: Building a heap from an unsorted array of n elements costs:
options: O(n) with bottom-up heapify
O(n log n) always
O(log n)
O(n²)
questions.explanation: Most nodes sit near the leaves and sift down only a little; the series sums to O(n). Inserting one at a time is O(n log n).

questions.prompt: To keep the k largest elements of a stream, use:
options: A min-heap of size k
A max-heap of size k
A sorted list of everything
A hash set
questions.explanation: The root of a min-heap is the weakest survivor, so it is exactly what to evict when a better candidate arrives.

questions.prompt: Peeking at the minimum of a min-heap costs:
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: The heap property puts the minimum at the root. Removing it is O(log n) because of the sift-down that follows.

questions.prompt: A Bloom filter's defining trade-off is:
options: False positives are possible, false negatives are not
It stores the keys but slowly
It never errs but uses more memory
It only works on integers
questions.explanation: It keeps bits, not keys, so "maybe present" can be wrong while "definitely absent" is always right — ideal as a cheap pre-filter.

quiz.title: DP & Greedy
quiz.description: States, recurrences and when greedy is provably safe.

questions.prompt: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has:
options: Optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems
Only optimal substructure
Sorted input
No recursion
questions.explanation: Without overlap, plain divide and conquer is enough — memoisation would store entries never read twice.

questions.prompt: Greedy coin change fails on coins [1, 3, 4] with amount 6 because:
options: Taking 4 first forces 4+1+1, while 3+3 uses fewer coins
6 cannot be made at all
The coins are unsorted
It only fails with negative amounts
questions.explanation: The locally biggest coin is not globally safe here. Canonical systems like [1, 5, 10, 25] happen to be greedy-safe; arbitrary ones are not.

questions.prompt: 0/1 Knapsack differs from Fractional Knapsack in that:
options: Items cannot be split, so greedy by value/weight is not optimal
It has no capacity limit
It allows negative weights
It is solved in O(1)
questions.explanation: Splitting is what makes the greedy exchange argument valid. Whole items require a DP table over capacities.

questions.prompt: In interval scheduling, the greedy choice that maximises how many intervals fit is:
options: Pick the interval that finishes earliest
Pick the shortest interval
Pick the one starting earliest
Pick the one overlapping fewest others
questions.explanation: Earliest finish leaves the most room for what follows, provable by an exchange argument. Earliest start is the classic wrong answer.

questions.prompt: Memoised recursion (top-down) versus tabulation (bottom-up):
options: Same complexity; top-down only computes reachable states, bottom-up avoids stack depth
Top-down is always faster
Bottom-up cannot handle 2D states
They solve different problem classes
questions.explanation: Choose top-down for sparse state spaces, bottom-up when deep recursion risks overflow or rolling arrays can cut space.

questions.prompt: Space in a 2D DP can often drop to O(min(m, n)) when:
options: Each cell depends only on the previous row (or column)
The table holds only zeroes and ones
The recurrence is linear
The inputs are sorted
questions.explanation: With a one-row dependency you can roll a single array forward — the trick used in LCS, edit distance and unique paths.

questions.prompt: To merge every overlapping interval in a list of [start, end] pairs, sort by start and then:
options: Extend the last kept interval's end whenever the next start is ≤ that end
Drop any interval whose start is inside the previous one
Sort by end instead and keep the earliest finisher
Compare every interval against every other
questions.explanation: Sorting by start means anything overlapping the current interval comes next, so one pass suffices: extend the end on overlap, otherwise start a new interval. O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) after. Sorting by end is the *scheduling* greedy — it maximises how many intervals fit, a different question.

quiz.title: Complexity Analysis
quiz.description: Big-O, amortized cost and space trade-offs.

questions.prompt: O(2n² + 100n + 5000) simplifies to:
options: O(n²)
O(2n²)
O(n² + n)
questions.explanation: Big-O drops constants and lower-order terms — they stop mattering as n grows.

questions.prompt: Two nested loops both running to n, where the inner starts at the outer's index, cost:
options: O(n²) — roughly n²/2 iterations
O(n)
O(n log n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: n + (n-1) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2, and the constant ½ drops out.

questions.prompt: Amortized O(1) means:
options: Averaged over a sequence of operations, each costs constant time
Every single operation is constant time
The best case is constant
It is constant only for small n
questions.explanation: Individual operations may be expensive — like a resize copy — as long as their cost is paid for by many cheap ones.

questions.prompt: A recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) solves to:
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(n²)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: log n levels of O(n) merging — the merge sort recurrence, and the Master Theorem's balanced case.

questions.prompt: Which is the space complexity of recursive DFS on a balanced binary tree?
options: O(log n) for the call stack
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Only the current root-to-node path is live. A degenerate tree pushes this to O(n).

questions.prompt: Worst case is a stronger guarantee than average case because:
options: It holds for every input, with no distributional assumption
It is always tighter
It ignores constants
It applies only to sorted input
questions.explanation: Average case assumes an input distribution that adversarial or real-world data may violate — quicksort's O(n²) worst case is the classic example.

quiz.title: Recursion & Backtracking
quiz.description: Base cases, call-stack cost, pruning and un-choosing.

questions.prompt: A recursion that never reaches its base case fails with:
options: A stack overflow — each call keeps a frame alive
A heap overflow
A wrong answer, but no crash
An infinite loop with constant memory
questions.explanation: Every pending call holds a stack frame with its locals and return address. Without a base case the frames accumulate until the stack is exhausted.

questions.prompt: Naive recursive Fibonacci runs in exponential time because:
options: The same subproblems are recomputed across separate branches
Each call allocates a new array
Addition on large integers is slow
The recursion depth is exponential
questions.explanation: fib(n-2) is recomputed inside both fib(n-1) and the direct call, so the tree has ~2ⁿ nodes while the depth is only n. Memoising collapses it to O(n).

questions.prompt: The step that makes backtracking different from plain recursion is:
options: Undoing the choice after exploring it, so the state is clean for the next branch
Caching every partial solution
Sorting the candidates first
Using a queue instead of the call stack
questions.explanation: Choose, explore, un-choose. Mutating shared state without the un-choose step leaks a branch's decisions into its siblings.

questions.prompt: In N-Queens, checking a candidate square against columns and both diagonals before recursing is:
options: Pruning — it cuts an entire subtree that cannot contain a solution
Memoisation
A greedy choice
Only a constant-factor speedup
questions.explanation: Rejecting a placement early removes every arrangement built on top of it. Pruning is what makes backtracking usable on search spaces that are exponential on paper.

questions.prompt: Generating all subsets of n distinct elements costs at least:
options: O(2ⁿ) — one per subset
O(n²)
O(n log n)
O(n!)
questions.explanation: Each element is in or out, so there are 2ⁿ subsets. Any algorithm that must emit them all is bounded below by the output size.

questions.prompt: When generating permutations of an array containing duplicates, the standard fix is to:
options: Sort first, then skip a candidate equal to its predecessor at the same depth
Store every permutation in a set at the end
Recurse only on the distinct prefix
Swap in reverse order
questions.explanation: Sorting groups equal values together; skipping a repeat at the same recursion level emits each distinct arrangement once. De-duplicating at the end works but wastes exponential effort first.

quiz.title: Bit Manipulation
quiz.description: Masks, XOR pairing, low-bit tricks and bitmask states.

questions.prompt: x & (x - 1) evaluates to:
options: x with its lowest set bit cleared
x with its lowest set bit isolated
x with every bit flipped
x doubled
questions.explanation: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and everything below it to 1; the AND then clears that bit. Looping on it counts set bits in O(popcount) steps.

questions.prompt: In an array where every value appears twice except one, XOR-ing all values yields:
options: The unique value — pairs cancel to 0
Zero
The sum of the duplicates
The largest value
questions.explanation: XOR is associative and commutative with a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a, so every pair vanishes and only the lone value survives. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.prompt: To test whether bit i of x is set:
options: x & i
questions.explanation: Shift the bit down to position 0 and mask it. `x | (1 << i)` sets the bit and `x ^ (1 << i)` toggles it — neither reports its current value.

questions.prompt: x & -x isolates the lowest set bit because two's complement negation:
options: Inverts every bit then adds 1, leaving the lowest set bit and everything above it inverted
Only changes the sign bit
Shifts the value right by one
Is identical to bitwise NOT
questions.explanation: -x = ~x + 1. The carry from the +1 stops at the lowest set bit, so x and -x agree on exactly that bit — the AND leaves it alone and zeroes the rest. Fenwick trees use it to walk parents.

questions.prompt: A bitmask DP over n items typically has how many states?
options: 2ⁿ — one per subset of items
n²
n log n
n!
questions.explanation: The mask encodes which items are already used, so the state space is every subset. That is why bitmask DP is practical only for roughly n ≤ 20.

questions.prompt: Which check tells you a positive integer x is a power of two?
questions.explanation: A power of two has exactly one set bit, and clearing the lowest set bit then leaves zero. `x % 2 == 0` only tests evenness — 6 passes it and is not a power of two.

quiz.title: String Matching
quiz.description: Prefix functions, rolling hashes, palindromes and tries.

questions.prompt: Naive substring search of a pattern of length m in text of length n is worst-case:
options: O(n · m)
O(n + m)
O(n log m)
O(m log n)
questions.explanation: Every one of ~n alignments can compare up to m characters before failing — "aaaa…ab" in "aaaa…a" hits exactly that. Smarter algorithms reuse the failed comparisons instead of discarding them.

questions.prompt: KMP's prefix table stores, for each position, the length of:
options: The longest proper prefix that is also a suffix
The longest repeated character run
The remaining pattern
The hash of the prefix
questions.explanation: That length says how far the pattern can slide on a mismatch without re-checking characters already matched, giving O(n + m) overall with no backtracking in the text.

questions.prompt: Rabin-Karp degrades to O(n · m) when:
options: Hash collisions are frequent, forcing a character-by-character verify each time
The pattern is short
The alphabet is large
The text is already sorted
questions.explanation: The rolling hash makes each window O(1), but equal hashes must still be verified. A bad modulus or an adversarial text turns every window into a full comparison.

questions.prompt: Manacher's algorithm finds the longest palindromic substring in:
options: O(n), by reusing mirrored radii inside the current palindrome
O(n log n), via binary search
O(n²), same as expand-around-center
O(n · m)
questions.explanation: Each center's radius starts from its mirror's already-known radius, so the right boundary only moves forward — total work is linear. Expand-around-center is the O(n²) fallback.

questions.prompt: A trie holding k words of average length L answers a prefix query in:
options: O(prefix length) — independent of k
O(k)
O(k · L)
O(log k)
questions.explanation: Lookup walks one node per prefix character, so the dictionary size does not enter the cost. The price is memory: a node per distinct prefix.

questions.prompt: To search a text for many patterns at once in one pass, use:
options: Aho-Corasick — a trie of all patterns plus failure links
KMP, run once per pattern
Binary search over the text
A suffix array of each pattern
questions.explanation: Failure links generalise KMP's prefix table to a whole trie, so one scan reports every occurrence of every pattern in O(n + total pattern length + matches).

quiz.title: Math & Number Theory
quiz.description: GCD, modular arithmetic, fast power and primes.

questions.prompt: The Euclidean algorithm computes gcd(a, b) in:
options: O(log min(a, b)) — the remainder at least halves every two steps
O(min(a, b))
O(√a)
O(a · b)
questions.explanation: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), and a mod b < a/2 whenever b ≤ a/2 — otherwise the next step drops it. Either way two iterations halve the pair.

questions.prompt: Fast exponentiation computes aⁿ using about how many multiplications?
options: log₂ n
n
√n
n log n
questions.explanation: Square-and-multiply halves the exponent each step: a^n = (a^(n/2))² for even n, times one extra a for odd n. One squaring per bit of n.

questions.prompt: Products are taken modulo a prime at every step of a computation mainly to:
options: Keep intermediate values inside machine word range and avoid overflow
Make the result larger
Speed up addition
Guarantee the result is prime
questions.explanation: Modular reduction distributes over + and ×, so reducing early gives the same answer while bounding every intermediate below the modulus.

questions.prompt: The Sieve of Eratosthenes marks all primes below n in:
options: O(n log log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n √n)
questions.explanation: Each prime p crosses out n/p entries, and the sum of 1/p over primes below n grows like log log n. Trial division per number would be O(n √n).

questions.prompt: With prime modulus p, the modular inverse of a is a^(p-2) mod p because of:
options: Fermat's little theorem — a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p)
The Chinese remainder theorem
The binomial theorem
Wilson's theorem
questions.explanation: From a^(p-1) ≡ 1, multiplying both sides by a⁻¹ gives a⁻¹ ≡ a^(p-2). Combined with fast power that is an O(log p) inverse — the usual trick for division under a modulus.

questions.prompt: Karatsuba multiplies two n-digit numbers in O(n^1.585) by:
options: Replacing four half-size multiplications with three plus additions
Using a lookup table of digit products
Converting both numbers to binary first
Multiplying digit by digit in parallel
questions.explanation: T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) solves to n^log₂3 ≈ n^1.585. The saved multiplication is recovered from the other two products with cheap additions.

quiz.title: ML Foundations
quiz.description: Bias/variance, loss functions and evaluation.

questions.prompt: A model with low training error and high test error is:
options: Overfitting — high variance
Underfitting — high bias
Perfectly regularised
Undertrained
questions.explanation: It memorised noise specific to the training set. Regularisation, more data, or a simpler model close the gap.

questions.prompt: Linear regression minimises which loss by default?
options: Mean squared error
Cross-entropy
Hinge loss
KL divergence
questions.explanation: Squared error has a closed-form solution and penalises large residuals quadratically — which also makes it outlier-sensitive.

questions.prompt: Logistic regression is used for classification because it:
options: Squashes a linear score into a probability with the sigmoid
Fits a straight line to class labels
Requires no training
Always produces a hard 0 or 1
questions.explanation: The linear score becomes a calibrated probability, trained with cross-entropy rather than squared error.

questions.prompt: On a heavily imbalanced dataset, accuracy misleads because:
options: Always predicting the majority class already scores high
It cannot be computed
It ignores the training set
It requires probabilities
questions.explanation: At 99% negatives a trivial model scores 99%. Precision, recall, F1 or AUC expose what it actually missed.

questions.prompt: k-NN is called a lazy learner because it:
options: Does no work at training time and all of it at prediction time
Converges slowly
Uses a small k
Ignores distant points
questions.explanation: It stores the training set and searches neighbours per query, so prediction cost grows with the dataset.

questions.prompt: PCA reduces dimensionality by projecting onto:
options: The directions of greatest variance
The axes with the smallest values
Randomly chosen axes
The class boundaries
questions.explanation: Top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix retain the most information. It is unsupervised, so it can discard a low-variance but discriminative direction.

quiz.title: Deep Learning
quiz.description: Backpropagation, activations and regularisation.

questions.prompt: Backpropagation computes gradients by:
options: Applying the chain rule backwards through the network
Perturbing each weight and re-running the forward pass
Randomly sampling gradients
Inverting the weight matrices
questions.explanation: One backward pass reuses cached forward activations to get every gradient — finite differences would cost one forward pass per weight.

questions.prompt: A network with only linear activations is equivalent to:
options: A single linear layer, no matter the depth
A decision tree
A convolutional network
A universal approximator
questions.explanation: Composing linear maps yields a linear map. Non-linearity is what depth actually buys.

questions.prompt: ReLU is preferred over sigmoid in hidden layers mainly because it:
options: Does not saturate for positive inputs, easing vanishing gradients
Is bounded between 0 and 1
Is smooth everywhere
Guarantees convergence
questions.explanation: Sigmoid gradients shrink toward zero at both tails, stalling deep networks. ReLU's own failure mode is dead units on the negative side.

questions.prompt: Dropout regularises by:
options: Randomly zeroing activations during training so no unit is relied on alone
Removing layers permanently
Shrinking the learning rate
Discarding training examples
questions.explanation: It approximates averaging many thinned networks. Dropout is disabled at inference, with activations scaled to compensate.

questions.prompt: A CNN suits images because convolution provides:
options: Local receptive fields and shared weights, giving translation equivariance
Full connectivity between all pixels
Guaranteed rotation invariance
Sequence modelling
questions.explanation: One kernel is reused across the image, cutting parameters massively and detecting a feature wherever it appears.

questions.prompt: LSTMs handle long sequences better than vanilla RNNs because they:
options: Carry a gated cell state that lets gradients flow further
Process the sequence in parallel
Use convolutions internally
Have fewer parameters
questions.explanation: Gates control what is written, kept and read, easing vanishing gradients. Transformers later removed recurrence altogether for parallelism.

quiz.title: NLP & RL
quiz.description: Embeddings, attention, rewards and policies.

questions.prompt: Word embeddings improve on one-hot encoding because they:
options: Place similar words near each other in a dense low-dimensional space
Use less training data
Are always sparse
Require no vocabulary
questions.explanation: One-hot vectors are equidistant, encoding no similarity. Embeddings put semantic structure into the geometry.

questions.prompt: TF-IDF down-weights a term that:
options: Appears in nearly every document
Appears rarely overall
Is long
Appears at the start of a document
questions.explanation: The inverse document frequency factor suppresses ubiquitous terms, which carry little discriminative signal.

questions.prompt: Self-attention lets a transformer:
options: Relate every token to every other in one layer, in parallel
Process tokens strictly left to right
Avoid needing positional information
Work only on fixed-length input
questions.explanation: Direct token-to-token paths remove recurrence, at O(n²) cost in sequence length. Positional encodings are added back because attention is order-agnostic.

questions.prompt: In an MDP, the discount factor γ controls:
options: How much future rewards count relative to immediate ones
The learning rate
The exploration probability
The size of the state space
questions.explanation: γ near 0 is myopic; near 1 is far-sighted and also keeps returns finite in continuing tasks.

questions.prompt: Q-learning is called off-policy because it:
options: Learns the greedy policy's values while behaving with a different, exploratory policy
Never updates its policy
Requires a model of the environment
Only works offline
questions.explanation: The update uses max over next actions regardless of what was actually taken. SARSA, which uses the action taken, is the on-policy counterpart.

questions.prompt: Experience replay in DQN mainly exists to:
options: Break the correlation between consecutive samples and reuse past data
Increase the discount factor
Remove the need for a target network
Make the policy deterministic
questions.explanation: Sequential transitions are highly correlated, which destabilises gradient updates. Sampling a buffer restores something closer to i.i.d. data.

quiz.title: Transformers & LLMs
quiz.description: Attention cost, positional information, pretraining and decoding.

questions.prompt: Self-attention over a sequence of length n costs:
options: O(n²) — every token attends to every other
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: The score matrix is n × n, which is why long-context models need sparse, linear or flash-attention variants.

questions.prompt: Transformers need positional encodings because attention is:
options: Permutation-invariant — it sees a set, not a sequence
Too slow otherwise
Unable to use embeddings
Restricted to short input
questions.explanation: Shuffling the input permutes the output identically. Position must be injected, by sinusoids, learned vectors or rotary embeddings.

questions.prompt: Dividing attention scores by √d prevents:
options: Large dot products pushing softmax into a saturated, low-gradient regime
Numerical underflow in the values
The keys and queries from differing in size
Overfitting
questions.explanation: Dot products grow with dimension. Unscaled, softmax approaches one-hot and gradients vanish.

questions.prompt: Multi-head attention helps because different heads can:
options: Attend to different relationships in parallel subspaces
Process longer sequences
Remove the need for feed-forward layers
Guarantee interpretability
questions.explanation: Each head projects into its own subspace, so one may track syntax while another tracks coreference. A single head must average all of it.

questions.prompt: Greedy decoding differs from sampling in that it:
options: Always takes the highest-probability token, producing repetitive but stable text
Is slower
Requires a larger model
Ignores the softmax
questions.explanation: Determinism costs diversity — hence temperature, top-k and nucleus sampling as middle grounds.

questions.prompt: Subword tokenisation such as BPE mainly solves:
options: Out-of-vocabulary words, by splitting rare words into known pieces
The quadratic cost of attention
Positional encoding
Gradient vanishing
questions.explanation: Word-level vocabularies map anything unseen to a single unknown token. Subwords keep rare words representable at a bounded vocabulary size.

quiz.title: RL Algorithms
quiz.description: Value versus policy methods, stability tricks and exploration.

questions.prompt: The difference between Q-learning and SARSA is that SARSA's target uses:
options: The action actually taken next, making it on-policy
A discount factor of 1
No reward term
A neural network
questions.explanation: Q-learning bootstraps from max over next actions regardless of behaviour; SARSA follows its own policy, making it more conservative near cliffs.

questions.prompt: A target network in DQN exists to:
options: Hold the bootstrap target fixed for a while so training does not chase a moving goal
Double the batch size
Replace the replay buffer
Add exploration noise
questions.explanation: Without it the target shifts every gradient step, since the same network produces both prediction and target.

questions.prompt: Double DQN reduces which specific failure of DQN?
options: Overestimation bias from taking a max over noisy value estimates
Slow convergence on small state spaces
Excessive exploration
Memory usage
questions.explanation: It decouples action selection from evaluation — one network picks the argmax, the other scores it.

questions.prompt: Policy-gradient methods are preferred over value-based ones when:
options: The action space is continuous or a stochastic policy is required
The state space is small
Rewards are always positive
The environment is deterministic
questions.explanation: A max over a continuous action space is intractable; policy methods parameterise the action distribution directly.

questions.prompt: A baseline subtracted from the return in REINFORCE:
options: Reduces gradient variance without biasing the estimate
Increases the learning rate
Guarantees convergence
Removes the need for a discount factor
questions.explanation: Any action-independent baseline has zero expected contribution. Using the value function as the baseline gives the advantage, which is actor-critic.

questions.prompt: PPO's clipped objective exists to:
options: Stop a single update from moving the policy too far from the one that collected the data
Speed up the forward pass
Eliminate the value network
Force deterministic actions
questions.explanation: Large policy jumps invalidate the sampled data and can collapse performance. Clipping is a cheap stand-in for TRPO's trust region.

quiz.title: Unsupervised Learning
quiz.description: Clustering assumptions, cluster counts and dimensionality reduction.

questions.prompt: k-means implicitly assumes clusters that are:
options: Roughly spherical and similar in size, since it assigns by Euclidean distance to a centroid
Arbitrarily shaped and of any density
Nested inside one another
Linearly separable by a hyperplane
questions.explanation: Assignment to the nearest centroid carves space into convex cells, so elongated, ring-shaped or wildly unequal clusters get split or merged. Density-based methods handle those.

questions.prompt: Unlike k-means, DBSCAN:
options: Finds arbitrarily shaped clusters and labels low-density points as noise
Requires the cluster count up front
Always assigns every point to a cluster
Only works on two-dimensional data
questions.explanation: It grows clusters from dense neighbourhoods defined by eps and minPts, so shape is unconstrained and outliers stay unassigned. The cost is sensitivity to eps when densities vary.

questions.prompt: A silhouette score near 0 for a point means:
options: It sits on the boundary between two clusters
It is deep inside its cluster
It is definitely misassigned
The clustering is perfect
questions.explanation: Silhouette compares within-cluster distance to nearest-other-cluster distance: ≈1 is well inside, ≈0 is on the border, and negative suggests the point belongs to the neighbouring cluster.

questions.prompt: PCA components are chosen to:
options: Be orthogonal directions capturing maximum remaining variance
Maximise class separation using the labels
Preserve pairwise distances exactly
Minimise the number of features to exactly two
questions.explanation: PCA is unsupervised — it never sees labels. Each component is the highest-variance direction orthogonal to those already taken. LDA is the supervised, class-separating counterpart.

questions.prompt: Why must features be standardised before PCA?
options: Variance is scale-dependent, so a large-unit feature would dominate the components
PCA cannot handle negative numbers
It makes the covariance matrix square
It guarantees orthogonality
questions.explanation: A feature measured in metres versus kilometres changes its variance by 10⁶ without changing the information. Z-scoring puts every feature on comparable footing first.

questions.prompt: t-SNE plots should not be read as showing:
options: Meaningful distances between well-separated clusters
Local neighbourhood structure
Groups of similar points
Possible cluster counts to investigate
questions.explanation: t-SNE optimises a local neighbourhood objective, so gaps between clusters and cluster sizes carry little meaning and change with perplexity. Use it to explore, not to measure.

quiz.title: Computer Vision
quiz.description: Convolutions, receptive fields, detection and segmentation.

questions.prompt: A convolutional layer beats a fully connected one on images mainly because:
options: Shared kernels give translation equivariance with far fewer parameters
It uses a different activation function
It never overfits
Convolution is faster than matrix multiplication in all cases
questions.explanation: One small kernel sweeps the whole image, so a feature detected in one corner is detected anywhere, and parameter count depends on kernel size rather than image size.

questions.prompt: A 32×32 input through a 3×3 convolution with stride 1 and no padding produces:
questions.explanation: Output = (W - K + 2P)/S + 1 = (32 - 3 + 0)/1 + 1 = 30. 'Same' padding (P = 1) is what preserves 32×32.

questions.prompt: Pooling layers are used to:
options: Shrink the spatial map and add small-shift tolerance
Increase the number of channels
Add trainable parameters
Normalise activations across the batch
questions.explanation: Max pooling keeps the strongest response in each window, halving height and width with no parameters and widening the receptive field of later layers.

questions.prompt: ResNet's skip connections help train very deep networks because they:
options: Give gradients a short path back, so identity is easy to learn
Reduce the parameter count to zero in deep layers
Replace the need for an activation function
Force every layer to learn a different feature
questions.explanation: With y = F(x) + x, a block that learns nothing still passes x through unchanged, and the additive path carries gradient without repeated multiplication through weights.

questions.prompt: YOLO is faster than Faster R-CNN because it:
options: Predicts boxes and classes in a single pass instead of proposing regions first
Uses a smaller input image
Skips the convolutional backbone
Runs only on GPUs
questions.explanation: Single-stage detectors regress boxes directly on a grid; two-stage detectors run a proposal network and then classify each region. The trade has historically been speed versus small-object accuracy.

questions.prompt: Semantic segmentation differs from instance segmentation in that it:
options: Labels every pixel by class without separating individual objects
Outputs bounding boxes only
Works on video rather than images
Requires no labelled data
questions.explanation: Semantic segmentation gives all three sheep one 'sheep' mask; instance segmentation (Mask R-CNN) separates sheep 1, 2 and 3. Panoptic combines both.

quiz.title: Data Preprocessing
quiz.description: Imputation, encoding, scaling, imbalance and leakage.

questions.prompt: Fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting into train and test causes:
options: Data leakage — test statistics inform the training transform
Nothing; scaling is label-independent
Underfitting
A shape mismatch at predict time
questions.explanation: The mean and standard deviation carry information from held-out rows, so the reported test score is optimistic. Fit on train, then transform both.

questions.prompt: Label-encoding a nominal feature like city for a linear model is wrong because it:
options: Invents an ordering and a distance between categories
Produces too many columns
Cannot handle unseen categories
Makes the feature continuous-valued and therefore unscalable
questions.explanation: Mapping to 0, 1, 2 tells the model city 2 is 'twice' city 1 and closer to city 3. One-hot removes the false ordering; tree models are less affected but still split arbitrarily.

questions.prompt: Min-max scaling is preferred over z-scoring when:
options: A bounded range is required and outliers are already handled
The data has heavy outliers
The feature is normally distributed
The model is a decision tree
questions.explanation: Min-max maps to [0, 1] using the extremes, so a single outlier compresses everything else into a sliver. Z-scoring is the more robust default; trees need neither.

questions.prompt: SMOTE addresses class imbalance by:
options: Synthesising minority examples along segments between neighbours
Deleting majority rows at random
Reweighting the loss function
Duplicating minority rows exactly
questions.explanation: Interpolating between a minority point and its k nearest minority neighbours adds variety that plain duplication cannot. Apply it inside the training fold only, never before the split.

questions.prompt: Median imputation is preferred over mean imputation when the feature:
options: Is skewed or has outliers
Is perfectly symmetric
Has no missing values
Is categorical
questions.explanation: The mean is dragged by extreme values, so imputed rows land somewhere no real row sits. The median is robust; categoricals get the mode or an explicit 'missing' level.

questions.prompt: Recursive feature elimination selects features by:
options: Repeatedly fitting the model and dropping the weakest features
Ranking features by correlation once
Random sampling of feature subsets
