Removing features with missing values
questions.explanation: RFE is a wrapper method: it uses the model's own importances, refits after each removal, and therefore captures interactions that one-shot filters like chi-square miss — at a much higher compute cost.

quiz.title: AI/ML Mock Interview
quiz.description: Mixed ML, DL, NLP and RL questions under one clock.

questions.prompt: A model scores 0.99 training accuracy and 0.62 on validation. The first thing to try is:
options: Regularisation or more data — it is overfitting
A larger model
A higher learning rate
More training epochs
questions.explanation: The gap is variance, not bias. Dropout, weight decay, augmentation or more data close it; a bigger model widens it.

questions.prompt: Features on wildly different scales hurt k-NN and gradient descent because:
options: Distance and gradient steps become dominated by the largest-scale feature
The model cannot store them
Labels become unbalanced
It only affects tree models
questions.explanation: Standardising fixes both. Tree-based models are the ones genuinely scale-invariant.

questions.prompt: Validation data leaking into training typically shows up as:
options: Excellent validation scores that collapse in production
Training loss that never decreases
Exploding gradients
Slower epochs
questions.explanation: Fitting the scaler or selecting features on the full dataset before splitting is the usual cause — the split must come first.

questions.prompt: Training loss decreasing while gradients in early layers approach zero indicates:
options: Vanishing gradients — the early layers have effectively stopped learning
A learning rate that is too high
Label noise
Too small a batch size
questions.explanation: Saturating activations and depth compound the shrinkage. ReLU, residual connections and normalisation are the standard remedies.

questions.prompt: For a text classifier with a small labelled dataset, the strongest first move is usually:
options: Fine-tune a pretrained language model
Train a transformer from scratch
Use one-hot word vectors
Increase the vocabulary size
questions.explanation: Pretraining supplies the language knowledge the small dataset cannot. Training from scratch needs orders of magnitude more data.

questions.prompt: An RL agent that gets stuck repeating one mediocre action most likely needs:
options: More exploration — a higher ε, entropy bonus or optimistic initialisation
A smaller discount factor
A larger replay buffer only
A deterministic policy
questions.explanation: Premature convergence on a locally good action is an exploration failure — the agent never sampled the better one often enough to value it.

quiz.title: Optimizers & Training
quiz.description: Momentum, adaptive rates, schedules and the losses they minimize.

questions.prompt: Momentum in SGD helps mainly by:
options: Accumulating a velocity term that smooths oscillation across ravines and speeds convergence
Increasing the learning rate every step
Reducing the number of parameters
Removing the need for a loss function
questions.explanation: A velocity term exponentially averages past gradients, damping oscillation across steep, narrow ravines and carrying speed through flat regions plain SGD would crawl across.

questions.prompt: AdaGrad's per-parameter learning rate eventually stalls training because it:
options: Accumulates squared gradients monotonically, so the effective rate only shrinks and never recovers
Resets to the initial rate every epoch
Ignores sparse gradients entirely
Requires a fixed batch size
questions.explanation: The denominator sums squared gradients since step one, so it grows without bound and the effective rate decays toward zero — fine for sparse features early on, fatal for long training runs.

questions.prompt: RMSprop fixes AdaGrad's vanishing rate by:
options: Replacing the cumulative sum with an exponential moving average of squared gradients
Removing the square root from the update
Freezing the learning rate after warmup
Averaging gradients across parameters instead of time
questions.explanation: A moving average forgets old gradients, so the accumulator can shrink again as gradients shrink, keeping the effective rate from decaying to zero the way AdaGrad's running sum does.

questions.prompt: Adam's bias-correction terms (dividing by 1 - β^t) matter most:
options: In the first few steps, when the moving averages are still biased toward zero
Only after the learning rate has decayed to zero
Only when the batch size is 1
Never — they are a no-op given the default betas
questions.explanation: Both moment estimates are initialised at zero, so early updates are biased small; the correction divides that bias out. By later steps 1 - β^t → 1 and the correction fades on its own.

questions.prompt: AdamW differs from Adam with L2 regularisation added to the loss because it:
options: Decouples weight decay from the gradient, so it isn't scaled by Adam's adaptive per-parameter rate
Removes momentum entirely
Uses a larger default learning rate
Only decays weights in the last layer
questions.explanation: L2-in-the-loss gets folded into the gradient and then divided by Adam's adaptive denominator, so parameters with large gradient history decay less. AdamW applies decay directly to the weights, outside that division.

questions.prompt: For softmax + cross-entropy, the gradient of the loss with respect to the logits simplifies to:
options: Predicted probabilities minus the one-hot label
The label minus the prediction, squared
The log of the predicted probability
Zero at every logit except the true class
questions.explanation: Softmax's Jacobian and cross-entropy's log cancel almost entirely, leaving p - y at each logit — the exact reason the pairing is used instead of, say, softmax with MSE.

quiz.title: Activation Functions
quiz.description: ReLU, sigmoid, GELU and the saturation, dead-unit trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25, which means:
options: Stacking many sigmoid layers multiplies gradients below 1 repeatedly, vanishing in deep networks
Sigmoid outputs can exceed 1
Sigmoid is unbounded
The gradient is constant regardless of input
questions.explanation: σ'(x) peaks at 0.25 when x = 0 and shrinks toward both tails. Chain-ruling through many such layers multiplies several numbers under 1, so early-layer gradients vanish — the classic reason deep nets avoided sigmoid hidden layers.

questions.prompt: Tanh is generally preferred over sigmoid in hidden layers because it:
options: Is zero-centred, so gradients on the next layer's weights aren't all pushed the same sign
Has no saturating regions
Is cheaper to compute
Outputs only positive values
questions.explanation: Sigmoid's always-positive output means every weight gradient in the next layer shares the same sign, forcing a zig-zag update path. Tanh's zero-centred range avoids that, though it still saturates at both ends.

questions.prompt: A 'dead' ReLU unit is one that:
options: Outputs zero for every input in the training set, so its gradient is permanently zero
Has a negative weight
Only activates for negative inputs
Has been pruned from the network
questions.explanation: If a large gradient step pushes a unit's pre-activation negative for every training example, ReLU's flat zero region on that side means the gradient is exactly zero and no update can ever revive it.

questions.prompt: Leaky ReLU addresses dying units by:
options: Giving negative inputs a small non-zero slope instead of flattening to exactly zero
Clipping positive inputs at 1
Adding a learnable bias to every neuron
Replacing the negative branch with an exponential
questions.explanation: A small fixed slope (e.g. 0.01) on the negative side keeps the gradient non-zero there, so a unit pushed negative can still receive updates and recover. PReLU makes that slope learnable instead of fixed.

questions.prompt: GELU differs from ReLU mainly in that it:
options: Weights each input by its probability under a Gaussian, giving a smooth, non-monotone curve near zero
Is a hard threshold at zero
Has no negative outputs at all
Requires no learned parameters, unlike ReLU
questions.explanation: GELU multiplies the input by the standard normal CDF evaluated at that input, so small negative values pass through partially rather than being hard-zeroed — the smooth curve transformers default to.

questions.prompt: Unlike ReLU or sigmoid, softmax needs a full Jacobian matrix (not a single derivative) for backprop because:
options: Each output depends on every input logit, not just the corresponding one
Softmax has no derivative
Softmax is applied before the loss, never after
It has more parameters than other activations
questions.explanation: Every softmax output is normalised by the sum over all logits, so changing one logit shifts every output, not just its own — the gradient is an n×n matrix, though it collapses to a simple form when paired with cross-entropy.

quiz.title: Arrays & Strings Warm-up
quiz.description: Indexing, two pointers, windows and counting — the first questions most screens open with.

questions.prompt: Reading arr[i] from an array of n elements costs:
options: O(1) — the address is computed straight from the index
O(i) — it walks from the start to position i
O(log n) — it binary-searches for the index
O(n) — the array is copied before reading
questions.explanation: Array elements sit side by side in memory, so element i lives at base + i × size. One multiplication and one read — no walking.

questions.prompt: Rotate nums right by k steps, in place with O(1) extra space. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 2 → [4, 5, 1, 2, 3].
options: Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k and the last n − k (after k %= n)
Move the last element to the front, k times
Copy into a new array at index (i + k) % n
Sort the array, then shift it
questions.explanation: Solve: reverse all → [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]; reverse the first 2 → [4, 5, 3, 2, 1]; reverse the rest → [4, 5, 1, 2, 3]. O(n), O(1). Moving one element k times is O(n·k); the copy is right but uses O(n) space.

questions.prompt: Given a sorted array, remove the duplicates in place and return how many unique values remain.
options: A slow write pointer copies nums[i] only when it differs from the last value written
Insert every value into a hash set and return its size
Delete each duplicate by shifting the rest of the array left
Binary search for each value's last copy
questions.explanation: Solve: w = 1; for i in 1 until n: if nums[i] != nums[w − 1], nums[w++] = nums[i]. Return w. Sorted input puts duplicates next to each other, so one comparison is enough. The hash set gives the count but leaves the array unchanged; shifting is O(n²).

questions.prompt: Is "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" a palindrome if you ignore case and punctuation? Best check:
options: Two pointers that skip non-letters and compare lowercase characters
Reverse the whole string, punctuation included, and compare
Count every letter and check all counts are even
Remove the vowels, then compare with the reverse
questions.explanation: Move left and right inward, skipping anything that is not a letter or digit, and compare lowercased characters. Reversing with punctuation fails on the comma placement; letter counts only tell you whether some rearrangement could be a palindrome.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a fitness app stores a week of daily step counts. The user taps "best day". How do you find it?
options: One pass keeping the largest value seen so far — O(n)
Sort the week, then take the last element — O(n log n)
Compare every day against every other day — O(n²)
Binary search for the maximum — O(log n)
questions.explanation: Solve: best = steps[0]; for each day, if steps[d] > best, best = steps[d]. One pass, O(1) memory. Sorting works but does more work than needed and loses which day it was; binary search needs sorted data, which step counts are not.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a scores list uses 0 for "absent". Move every 0 to the end while keeping the other scores in their original order, in place:
options: A write pointer copies each non-zero forward, then fills the tail with zeros
Sort the array in descending order
Remove each zero and append it, shifting the array every time
Swap each zero with the current last element
questions.explanation: Solve: w = 0; for each value v, if v ≠ 0 then a[w++] = v. Afterwards set a[w..n−1] = 0. O(n), O(1) space, order kept. Sorting reorders the scores; remove-and-append is O(n²); swapping with the last element scrambles the order.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a sales dashboard is asked "total sales from day l to day r" thousands of times. Best approach:
options: Precompute prefix sums once; each query is prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l]
Loop from l to r and add, for every query
Sort the sales, then add the middle section
Precompute and store every possible (l, r) range sum
questions.explanation: Solve: prefix[0] = 0 and prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + sales[i]. Any range is then two lookups and a subtraction — O(n) setup, O(1) per query. Looping is O(n) per query; storing every range costs O(n²) memory; sorting destroys the day order.

questions.prompt: Are "listen" and "silent" anagrams? The cleanest O(n) check:
options: Count the letters of both words and compare the counts
Check that the first and last letters match
Compare the lengths only
Check that each word is a palindrome
questions.explanation: Anagrams use exactly the same letters the same number of times. A 26-slot count array (or a map) does it in one pass per word. Sorting both words and comparing also works, at O(n log n). Equal lengths is necessary but nowhere near sufficient.

questions.prompt: Scenario: find the highest total over any k consecutive days of revenue. Best approach:
options: Slide a size-k window: add the entering day, subtract the leaving one — O(n)
Re-add all k days at every starting position — O(n·k)
Sort the days and add the k largest
Find the single best day and add its neighbours
questions.explanation: Solve: sum the first k days, then for each next day do sum += a[i] − a[i − k] and track the best. Every step is O(1). Sorting picks the k best days even when they are not consecutive, which answers a different question.

questions.prompt: Return the first character that appears exactly once in a string:
options: Two passes: count every character, then return the first with count 1 — O(n)
Sort the string and return the first character with no equal neighbour
Return the first character that differs from the one after it
Binary search the character positions
questions.explanation: Pass one fills a count map; pass two walks the original string in order and stops at the first count of 1. Sorting finds a unique character, but not the first one — it throws the original order away.

quiz.title: Hash Maps & Sets Warm-up
quiz.description: Lookups, counting and membership — the tool that turns most O(n²) answers into O(n).

questions.prompt: Average cost of looking up a key in a hash map:
options: O(1) on average — the key hashes straight to its bucket
O(log n) — keys are kept in sorted order
O(n) — every stored key is compared in turn
O(n log n) — the table is sorted on each lookup
questions.explanation: The hash function turns the key into a bucket index, so a lookup checks one bucket. Collisions can make one bucket long, which is why the worst case is O(n) — but a good hash and resizing keep the average at O(1).

questions.prompt: Two Sum on an unsorted array: find two indices whose values add up to a target, in O(n):
options: One pass: for each number, check whether target − number is already in a map
Sort the array, then binary search for every pair
Two nested loops over all pairs
Two pointers from both ends, without sorting
questions.explanation: Keep a map value → index of what you have seen. For each x, if target − x is in the map you have your pair; otherwise store x. O(n) time, O(n) space. Two pointers only work on sorted input, and nested loops are O(n²).

questions.prompt: Scenario: a signup form must instantly reject an email that is already registered, among 1,000,000 users. Store the emails in:
options: A hash set — each check is O(1) on average
An unsorted list scanned on every signup
A stack, popped until the email is found
A list that is re-sorted before each check
questions.explanation: Solve: normalise the email (trim, lowercase), then if set.contains(email) reject, else set.add(email). A scan is a million comparisons per signup; re-sorting is O(n log n) per signup; popping a stack destroys the data you are checking.

questions.prompt: Given [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2], return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers, in O(n).
options: 4 — put everything in a set, and count upwards only from numbers whose n − 1 is missing
6 — the number of distinct values
4 — sort and count the runs, which is O(n)
2 — the longest run of neighbours in the array
questions.explanation: Solve: for each x with x − 1 not in the set, count x, x + 1, … while they are present. Each number is counted once in total, so the whole thing is O(n). Sorting finds the same 4 (1, 2, 3, 4) but costs O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Given nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3] and k = 2, return the k most frequent values.
options: [1, 2] — count with a map, then bucket values by frequency (O(n)) or keep a size-k heap
[1, 1] — sort and take the first k
[3, 2] — the k largest values
[1, 2, 3] — every distinct value
questions.explanation: Solve: counts {1: 3, 2: 2, 3: 1}. Bucket sort: bucket[frequency] = values, then walk from the highest frequency down until you have k. A size-k min-heap gives O(n log k) and handles streaming input.

questions.prompt: Scenario: show how often each word appears in a 10,000-word article. Best approach:
options: Map each word to a counter and increment it as you read — O(n)
For each distinct word, rescan the whole article
Sort the words, then binary search for each one
Push every word onto a stack and count while popping
questions.explanation: Solve: for each word w (lowercased, punctuation stripped), counts[w] = counts.getOrDefault(w, 0) + 1. One pass. Sorting and counting adjacent runs also works at O(n log n); rescanning per word is O(n²).

questions.prompt: Does an unsorted array contain any duplicate? The O(n) check:
options: Insert each element into a hash set; stop when one is already present
Check whether the array's sum is odd
Compare each element only with its neighbour
Check whether the array is already sorted
questions.explanation: A set remembers everything seen so far, so the first repeat is caught the moment it arrives. Comparing neighbours only works after sorting (O(n log n)), because duplicates in unsorted data need not be adjacent.

questions.prompt: Group ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat"] into anagram groups. Key the map by:
options: Each word's letters in sorted order
Each word's length
Each word's first letter
Each word's number of vowels
questions.explanation: Anagrams sort to the same string: "eat", "tea" and "ate" all become "aet". Length, first letter and vowel count would all put "tan" and "eat" together, or split real anagrams apart.

questions.prompt: Scenario: show the mutual friends of two users, with m and n friends. Best approach:
options: Put one list in a hash set, then check each of the other user's friends — O(m + n)
Compare every friend with every other friend — O(m·n)
Merge both lists and remove duplicates
Sort both lists and return the longer one
questions.explanation: Solve: seen = set(friendsA); mutual = friendsB.filter { it in seen }. Build the set from the smaller list to save memory. Merging and removing duplicates gives the union — everyone either user knows — not the people they share.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't you change an object after using it as a hash map key?
options: Its hash changes, so later lookups search the wrong bucket and miss it
Maps copy their keys, so the change is silently ignored
Every language throws an exception when a key is mutated
It forces the map to sort itself again
questions.explanation: The entry was filed under the old hash. After the change, get() hashes to a different bucket and returns nothing, even though the entry is still in the map. Use immutable keys — strings, numbers, data classes with val fields.

quiz.title: Big-O Warm-up
quiz.description: Read a loop, name its cost, and check whether an approach fits the input size.

questions.prompt: A single loop from 0 to n doing constant work each time runs in:
options: O(n) — the body runs once per element
O(1) — a loop is a single statement
O(log n) — the counter grows every time
O(n²) — the loop compares every element
questions.explanation: n iterations × O(1) work = O(n). Double the input and the loop does twice the work — the definition of linear growth.

questions.prompt: for (i in 1..n) { var j = 1; while (j < n) j *= 2 } — the total cost:
options: O(n log n) — n outer iterations, each with about log₂ n doublings
O(n²) — two loops always multiply to n²
O(n) — the inner loop is constant
O(log n) — only the doubling matters
questions.explanation: Multiply the cost of each loop: the outer runs n times and the inner doubles j until it reaches n, about log₂ n times. Nested loops are only n² when both loops count up one at a time to n.

questions.prompt: for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) { … } — how many iterations?
options: O(log n) — i doubles, so it passes n after about log₂ n steps
O(n) — it still reaches n in the end
O(n/2) — it skips every other number
O(√n) — it grows faster than linear
questions.explanation: i takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8 … 2ᵏ, stopping when 2ᵏ ≥ n, so k ≈ log₂ n. For n = 1,000,000 that is only 20 iterations.

questions.prompt: for (x in items) { if (x in seenList) … } — both have n elements and seenList is a plain list. The cost:
options: O(n²) — `in` on a list is a hidden linear scan; a set makes it O(n)
O(n) — `in` is one operation
O(n log n) — the list is searched by halving
O(1) — both are fixed-size collections
questions.explanation: Library calls have costs too. contains() on a list checks each element; on a hash set it hashes once. Spotting a hidden O(n) call inside a loop is one of the most common interview fixes.

questions.prompt: A loop over array A (size n), followed by a separate loop over array B (size m):
options: O(n + m) — the loops run one after the other
O(n·m) — every pair of loops multiplies
O(max(n, m)²) — the longer loop dominates twice
O(n) — m can always be ignored
questions.explanation: Sequential work adds; nested work multiplies. You cannot drop m because B may be far bigger than A — keep both inputs in the answer.

questions.prompt: Scenario: an O(n²) report takes 1 second for 1,000 rows. Roughly how long for 2,000 rows?
options: About 4 seconds — doubling n quadruples n²
About 2 seconds — twice the rows, twice the time
About 1 second — the runtime is fixed
About 8 seconds — each row doubles the time
questions.explanation: Solve: (2,000 / 1,000)² = 2² = 4, so about 4 seconds. At 10,000 rows it would be 10² = 100 seconds — this is how you spot, before shipping, that a quadratic report will not scale.

questions.prompt: Scenario: n = 1,000,000 with a 1-second limit (about 10⁸ simple operations). Which complexity fits?
options: O(n log n) — about 2 × 10⁷ operations
O(n²) — about 10¹² operations
O(n³) — about 10¹⁸ operations
O(2ⁿ) — the fastest for large n
questions.explanation: Solve: plug n in. n log₂ n ≈ 10⁶ × 20 = 2 × 10⁷, well under 10⁸. n² = 10¹² is roughly 10,000 times over budget. Reading the constraints first tells you which algorithms are even worth trying.

questions.prompt: A function that copies its input array before processing it uses how much extra space?
options: O(n) — the copy holds all n elements
O(1) — a copy reuses the original's memory
O(log n) — only half the array is stored
O(n²) — each element is copied n times
questions.explanation: Extra (auxiliary) space counts memory beyond the input. A full copy is n more elements. Interviewers often ask whether you can drop it and work in place for O(1).

questions.prompt: T(n) = T(n / 2) + O(n) — for example, a function that does linear work and then recurses on half. It solves to:
options: O(n log n) — log n levels of O(n) work
O(log n) — the input halves every call
O(n²) — each call repeats the linear work
questions.explanation: Solve: the work shrinks geometrically, so the first call dominates and the total stays under 2n. O(n log n) needs two half-sized calls per level, as in merge sort's T(n) = 2T(n / 2) + O(n).

questions.prompt: var s = ""; for (c in chars) s += c — building a string of n characters this way costs:
options: O(n²) — each += copies the whole string so far; a StringBuilder makes it O(n)
O(n) — each append is constant
O(n log n) — the string doubles like an array
O(1) — strings are cached
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable in Java, Kotlin and Python, so s += c builds a new string: 1 + 2 + … + n = O(n²) characters copied. StringBuilder (or "".join) appends into a growing buffer in amortised O(1).

quiz.title: Stacks, Queues & Lists Warm-up
quiz.description: Pick the right container for everyday features — back buttons, print queues, undo.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a browser's Back button returns to the page you visited most recently. Store the history in:
options: A stack — the most recent page comes off first
A queue — the oldest page comes back first
A hash set — pages have no order
A sorted array — pages ordered by URL
questions.explanation: Solve: push each page when you navigate away; Back pops the top. Last in, first out is exactly "most recent first". A queue would take you back to the first page you opened.

questions.prompt: Scenario: an office printer must print jobs in the order they were sent. Use:
options: A queue — first in, first out
A stack — the newest job prints first
A heap keyed by page count
A hash map keyed by file name
questions.explanation: Solve: enqueue at the back when a job arrives; the printer dequeues from the front. Both are O(1). A stack would starve the earliest jobs; a heap by page count reorders them.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the Reverse Polish Notation tokens ["2", "1", "+", "3", "*"].
options: 9 — push numbers; on an operator pop two, apply it, push the result
6 — add up every number
7 — apply the operators right to left
5 — ignore the operators after the first
questions.explanation: Solve: push 2, push 1; '+' pops 1 and 2 and pushes 3; push 3; '*' pops 3 and 3 and pushes 9. The first value popped is the right-hand operand — that matters for '−' and '/'.

questions.prompt: Inserting a new node at the head of a singly linked list costs:
options: O(1) — point the new node at the old head, then move head
O(n) — every node shifts one position right
O(log n) — the list is searched for the right spot
O(n) — the tail must be found first
questions.explanation: node.next = head; head = node. Two pointer writes, nothing moves. That constant-time front insert is the main thing a linked list offers over an array.

questions.prompt: Reverse a singly linked list in place:
options: Walk it with prev, curr and next pointers, flipping each next pointer
Copy the values into an array, sort them descending, write them back
Swap the head and tail nodes only
Delete each node and re-insert it at the tail
questions.explanation: Loop: next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next. When curr is null, prev is the new head. O(n) time, O(1) space. Sorting descending reverses values only if they happened to be sorted.

questions.prompt: Find the middle node of a linked list in a single pass:
options: Slow pointer moves 1, fast moves 2; when fast reaches the end, slow is the middle
Jump straight to index n / 2
Reverse the list and take the new head
Count backwards from the tail
questions.explanation: Fast covers twice the distance, so it hits the end exactly when slow is halfway. Lists have no index access and singly linked lists cannot walk backwards, which rules out the other options.

questions.prompt: Remove the n-th node from the end of a linked list, in one pass.
options: Move a lead pointer n steps ahead, then advance both until the lead reaches the end
Reverse the list, delete the n-th node, then reverse it back
Jump straight to index length − n
Delete the head n times
questions.explanation: Solve: start both at a dummy head; move lead n + 1 steps; advance both until lead is null. The trailing pointer is now just before the target, so trail.next = trail.next.next. The dummy handles removing the head. Reversing twice works but takes three passes.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a text editor needs both Undo and Redo. Store the edits in:
options: Two stacks — undo pops from one and pushes onto the other
One queue shared by undo and redo
A single array scanned from the start
A hash map keyed by edit timestamp
questions.explanation: Solve: each edit pushes onto undoStack and clears redoStack. Undo: pop from undoStack, revert it, push onto redoStack. Redo: the reverse. Clearing redo on a new edit matters — otherwise redo would replay onto text that has changed since.

questions.prompt: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
options: Dummy head; repeatedly attach the smaller front node and advance that list — O(m + n)
Concatenate the lists, then sort the result
Alternate one node from each list
Insert each node of list two into list one using binary search
questions.explanation: Solve: tail = dummy; while both remain, attach the smaller head to tail and advance it; finally attach whatever is left. No new nodes are created. Alternating ignores the values, and binary search does not work on a linked list.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a support chat serves customers in arrival order, but VIP customers jump ahead. Use:
options: A priority queue (heap) ordered by priority, then arrival time
A plain stack
A plain FIFO queue
An unsorted array, picking a random customer
questions.explanation: Solve: key each customer as (isVip ? 0 : 1, arrivalTime) in a min-heap. Poll returns the earliest VIP, or the earliest regular customer if no VIP is waiting. O(log n) insert and poll. A plain queue ignores VIPs.

quiz.title: Recursion, Sorting & Search Warm-up
quiz.description: Recursion, binary search variants and one-pass sorting.

questions.prompt: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many different ways are there to climb 5 steps?
options: 8 — ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2), with ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2
5 — one way per step
questions.explanation: Solve: the last move was either a 1-step from stair n − 1 or a 2-step from n − 2, so the counts add: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. That is Fibonacci. Two variables give O(n) time and O(1) space; 2⁵ counts sequences that overshoot the top.

questions.prompt: sum(n) = n + sum(n − 1), with sum(0) = 0. What does sum(4) return?
questions.explanation: Unroll it: 4 + sum(3) = 4 + 3 + sum(2) = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + sum(0) = 10. Tracing a small input by hand is how you check recursive code before running it. (24 would be 4!, which multiplies.)

questions.prompt: Binary search only works when:
options: The data is sorted
The data has no duplicates
The array length is a power of two
The data fits in a hash map
questions.explanation: Each step compares with the middle and throws away the half that cannot contain the target. That is only safe when order tells you which side the target is on.

questions.prompt: Scenario: guess a number from 1 to 100; after each guess you hear "higher" or "lower". Worst-case guesses with the best strategy:
options: 7 — halve the range every guess (2⁷ = 128 ≥ 100)
10 — one guess per ten numbers
50 — half of the range
100 — one guess per number
questions.explanation: Solve: guess 50; "higher" leaves 51–100, so guess 75, and so on. The range goes 100 → 50 → 25 → 13 → 7 → 4 → 2 → 1: at most 7 guesses, which is ⌈log₂ 100⌉.

questions.prompt: Scenario: builds 1 to 1,000 are released in order; from some build onward they are all broken. Find the first broken build with the fewest tests:
options: Binary search on build number — about 10 tests
Test every build from the first — up to 1,000 tests
Test every other build — about 500 tests
Test only the newest build
questions.explanation: Solve: lo = 1, hi = 1000. While lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if broken(mid) then hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1. lo is the answer. Broken-ness is sorted (good…good, bad…bad), so you binary-search for the boundary, not for a value.

figure.caption: Builds in release order — only a few tested so far

questions.prompt: Sort [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0] (values 0, 1, 2 only) in one pass with O(1) extra space.
options: Three pointers low / mid / high: swap 0s to low and 2s to high
Counting sort — two passes
The built-in sort
Bubble sort
questions.explanation: Solve: while mid ≤ high: 0 → swap(low++, mid++); 1 → mid++; 2 → swap(mid, high--) and do not advance mid, because the swapped-in value is still unchecked. Counting sort is correct but takes two passes, which the question rules out.

questions.prompt: Return the minimum of a rotated sorted array such as [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], in O(log n).
options: Binary search: if nums[mid] > nums[hi], the minimum is right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left
Return the first element
A linear scan — the only correct way
Binary search for the value 0
questions.explanation: Solve: lo = 0, hi = n − 1; while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if nums[mid] > nums[hi] then lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid. Return nums[lo]. Comparing with nums[hi] tells you which half holds the drop. (Assumes distinct values.)

questions.prompt: Search an m × n matrix whose rows are sorted and each row starts above the previous row's end.
options: Treat it as one sorted array of m·n values and binary search — O(log(m·n))
Binary search each row separately — O(m log n)
Scan every cell — O(m·n)
Search only the diagonal
questions.explanation: Solve: lo = 0, hi = m·n − 1; index k maps to matrix[k / n][k % n]. Because each row continues where the last one ended, the flattened order is fully sorted. Searching row by row is correct but slower.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a leaderboard of 20 sorted scores gets one new score added at the end. Re-sort it with:
options: Insertion sort — nearly sorted input runs in close to O(n)
Selection sort — it always makes O(n²) comparisons
Bubble sort with no early exit
Shuffle it first, then sort
questions.explanation: Solve: insertion sort slides the new score left until it sits behind a larger one — at most 20 shifts. Everything else is already in place, so it barely does any work. Selection sort does the full O(n²) scan whatever the input.

questions.prompt: Scenario: list every possible play order for 3 songs. Approach and count:
options: Backtracking: pick an unused song, recurse, then un-pick — 3! = 6 orders
One loop over the songs — 3 orders
Sort the songs — 1 order
Binary search the songs — log₂ 3 orders
questions.explanation: Solve: at each position try every song not yet used, recurse to fill the rest, then remove it and try the next. 3 choices, then 2, then 1: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6. The un-pick step is what lets one list be reused for every branch.

quiz.title: Coding Round: Arrays & Hashing
quiz.description: Ten classic array and hashing problems, posed the way an interviewer asks them.

questions.prompt: Given nums, return an array where output[i] is the product of every element except nums[i] — in O(n), without division.
options: Prefix products left to right, then multiply in suffix products right to left
Multiply everything once, then divide by nums[i]
Nested loops multiplying every j ≠ i
Sort the array and multiply neighbours
questions.explanation: Solve: out[i] = product of everything left of i (one forward pass), then walk backwards with a running suffix product and multiply it in. [1, 2, 3, 4] → [24, 12, 8, 6]. O(n) time, O(1) extra besides the output. Division is banned, and it breaks on a zero anyway.

questions.prompt: Given nums, return every unique triplet [a, b, c] with a + b + c = 0.
options: Sort, fix each i, then two pointers over the rest, skipping repeated values — O(n²)
Three nested loops plus a set of sorted triplets — O(n³)
Hash every pair sum without sorting — O(n)
Binary search for the third value without sorting
questions.explanation: Solve: sort. For each i (skip if nums[i] == nums[i − 1]), set l = i + 1, r = n − 1; move l up if the sum is too small, r down if too big, and on a hit record it and skip duplicates on both sides. Sorting is what makes both the pointers and the de-duplication work.

questions.prompt: Given nums where one value appears more than n / 2 times, return it in O(n) time and O(1) space.
options: Boyer-Moore voting: keep a candidate and a counter
Return the middle element without sorting
Return the most frequent value in the first half
Return the maximum value
questions.explanation: Solve: count = 0; for each x, if count == 0 then candidate = x; count += (x == candidate) ? 1 : −1. The majority survives because it outnumbers everything else combined. Sorting and taking the middle also works, at O(n log n).

questions.prompt: nums1 has m values followed by n empty slots; nums2 has n values. Both are sorted. Merge nums2 into nums1 in place.
options: Fill from the back: write the larger of the two remaining tails at index m + n − 1
Fill from the front, shifting nums1 right on each insert
Append nums2, then bubble sort
Copy both arrays into a hash set
questions.explanation: Solve: i = m − 1, j = n − 1, k = m + n − 1. While j ≥ 0: if i ≥ 0 and nums1[i] > nums2[j], nums1[k--] = nums1[i--], else nums1[k--] = nums2[j--]. The back of nums1 is empty, so nothing is overwritten before it is read. O(m + n).

questions.prompt: Given a partly filled 9 × 9 Sudoku board, return whether it is valid so far (no repeat in any row, column or 3 × 3 box).
options: One pass with a set per row, column and box — box index = (r / 3) · 3 + c / 3
Solve the whole puzzle with backtracking first
Check that every row adds up to 45
Check only the two diagonals
questions.explanation: Solve: for each filled cell, try adding its digit to rows[r], cols[c] and boxes[(r / 3) · 3 + c / 3]; any failed add means invalid. 81 cells, constant work. Sums fail because duplicates can add to 45, and empty cells make the sum meaningless.

questions.prompt: Given nums (negatives allowed), return the largest product of any contiguous subarray.
options: Track both the max and min product ending here — a negative swaps them
Kadane's algorithm on sums
Multiply all the positive numbers
Sort and multiply the three largest
questions.explanation: Solve: for each x, if x < 0 swap hi and lo; then hi = max(x, hi · x), lo = min(x, lo · x), best = max(best, hi). The smallest (most negative) product can become the largest after one more negative. [2, 3, −2, 4] → 6.

questions.prompt: nums holds n distinct values from 0..n, so exactly one is missing. Return it in O(n) time and O(1) space.
options: Expected sum n(n + 1) / 2 minus the actual sum (or XOR every index with every value)
Sort, then binary search for 0
Always return n + 1
Return the smallest value
questions.explanation: Solve: 0 + 1 + … + n = n(n + 1) / 2; subtract what is there and the gap is the answer. The XOR version (i ^ nums[i] across all i, then ^ n) cancels every pair and cannot overflow.

questions.prompt: Given ransomNote and magazine, return whether the note can be built using each magazine letter at most once.
options: Count the magazine's letters, then decrement per note letter — fail if any count goes negative
Check that the note is a substring of the magazine
Check that both strings have the same length
Check that every note letter appears somewhere in the magazine
questions.explanation: Solve: counts = IntArray(26); for c in magazine counts[c]++; for c in note if (--counts[c] < 0) return false. O(n + m). "Appears somewhere" ignores counts: note "aa" with magazine "ab" would wrongly pass.

questions.prompt: Given an m × n matrix, return all its elements in spiral order.
options: Walk four boundaries (top, right, bottom, left), shrinking each one after its pass
Read row by row, reversing every other row
Read it diagonal by diagonal
Transpose it, then flatten
questions.explanation: Solve: top = 0, bottom = m − 1, left = 0, right = n − 1. Read the top row then top++, right column then right--, bottom row (if top ≤ bottom) then bottom--, left column (if left ≤ right) then left++. The two checks stop a single leftover row or column being read twice.

questions.prompt: Rotate an n × n image 90° clockwise, in place.
options: Transpose it, then reverse each row
Reverse each row, then transpose
Swap each pair of opposite corners only
Copy it into a new matrix — that counts as in place
questions.explanation: Solve: swap m[i][j] with m[j][i] for j > i (transpose), then reverse every row. Doing it the other way round — reverse rows, then transpose — rotates counter-clockwise. O(n²) time, O(1) space.

quiz.title: Coding Round: Linked Lists & Stacks
quiz.description: Pointer rewiring and stack problems — palindromes, intersections, decoding.

questions.prompt: Given the head of a singly linked list, return whether it is a palindrome, using O(1) extra space.
options: Find the middle with fast/slow pointers, reverse the second half, compare the halves
Copy the values into an array and use two pointers
Compare head and tail, walking to the tail each time
Reverse the whole list and compare it with itself
questions.explanation: Solve: slow and fast find the middle; reverse from slow onward; walk one pointer from the head and one from the reversed half, comparing values. Restore the list afterwards if the caller needs it. The array version is correct but uses O(n) space.

questions.prompt: Given the heads of two singly linked lists that may merge, return the node where they intersect (or null).
options: Two pointers; when one reaches the end, restart it at the other list's head — they meet at the intersection
Compare the node values position by position
Reverse both lists and compare their heads
Return the middle node of the longer list
questions.explanation: Solve: a = headA, b = headB; while a !== b, a = if (a == null) headB else a.next, and the same for b with headA. Each walks lenA + lenB, so they line up at the shared node, or both hit null. Compare nodes by reference — equal values do not mean a shared node.

questions.prompt: Two numbers are stored as linked lists of digits in reverse order: 2→4→3 is 342. Return their sum as a list.
options: Walk both lists digit by digit, carrying into the next node
Convert both lists to integers, add, convert back
Reverse both lists first, then add
Add only the first digits
questions.explanation: Solve: dummy head, carry = 0; while either list or carry remains: s = a + b + carry, append s % 10, carry = s / 10. 2→4→3 + 5→6→4 = 7→0→8 (342 + 465 = 807). Converting to integers overflows once the lists are longer than about 19 digits.

questions.prompt: Given a sorted linked list, delete the duplicates so each value appears once.
options: If curr.next has the same value, unlink it (curr.next = curr.next.next); otherwise advance
Put every value in a hash set and rebuild the list
Sort the list first
Delete the head until the values differ
questions.explanation: Solve: sorted means duplicates are neighbours, so one pointer is enough. Only advance curr when the next value differs — advancing after an unlink would skip a third copy. O(n), O(1) space.

questions.prompt: Simplify the Unix path "/a/./b/../../c/" to its canonical form.
options: Split on '/', push names, pop on '..', skip '.' and empty parts — result "/c"
Remove every '.' character — result "/a/b/c"
Keep only the last name — result "/c/"
Reverse the parts and join them
questions.explanation: Solve: parts a, ., b, .., .., c → push a, skip ., push b, pop b, pop a, push c. Join with '/' and prefix '/': "/c". A '..' on an empty stack stays at the root.

questions.prompt: Decode "3[a2[c]]", where k[s] means s repeated k times.
options: Two stacks (counts and partial strings); on ']' pop and repeat — "accaccacc"
Repeat each letter by the digit before it — "aaacc"
Delete the digits and brackets — "ac"
Expand only the outermost bracket — "a2[c]a2[c]a2[c]"
questions.explanation: Solve: digits build k; '[' pushes (k, current) and resets them; letters append to current; ']' pops (k, prev) and sets current = prev + current × k. Inner c → "cc", then "acc" × 3 = "accaccacc".

questions.prompt: Reorder a list L0→L1→…→Ln into L0→Ln→L1→Ln−1→…, in place.
options: Find the middle, reverse the second half, then weave the two halves together
Sort the list
Repeatedly walk to the tail and move it forward
Swap every adjacent pair
questions.explanation: Solve: three O(n) passes — fast/slow to split, iterative reverse of the second half, then alternate one node from each half. Walking to the tail every time is O(n²).

questions.prompt: Swap every two adjacent nodes: 1→2→3→4 becomes 2→1→4→3. Rewire pointers, do not swap values.
options: Dummy head, then rewire three pointers per pair and move prev on by two
Reverse the whole list
Sort the pairs in descending order
Move every even-position node to the front
questions.explanation: Solve: prev = dummy. While a pair exists: first = prev.next, second = first.next; first.next = second.next; second.next = first; prev.next = second; prev = first. The dummy removes the special case for the new head.

questions.prompt: Rotate a linked list right by k places (k may be larger than the length).
options: Get the length, link the tail to the head, then break the ring at length − k % length
Move the tail to the front k times
Reverse the list k times
Sort the list, then shift it
questions.explanation: Solve: one pass for length L and the tail; tail.next = head; walk L − k % L − 1 steps to the new tail, set newHead = newTail.next and newTail.next = null. Moving the tail k times is O(n·k), and k can be huge.

questions.prompt: Deep-copy a linked list where every node also has a random pointer to any node or null.
options: Map each old node to its copy (or interleave copies), then set next and random
Copy the next pointers only and leave random null
Copy the values into an array
Reuse the original nodes in the new list
questions.explanation: Solve: pass 1 creates copy[node] for every node; pass 2 sets copy[n].next = copy[n.next] and copy[n].random = copy[n.random]. The map solves the problem of a random pointer to a node not copied yet. Interleaving A→A'→B→B' does it in O(1) extra space.

quiz.title: Coding Round: Trees
quiz.description: Depth, symmetry, paths and BST building — the tree problems every screen opens with.

questions.prompt: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth.
options: Recursion: 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)), with an empty tree = 0
Count all the nodes
Follow the left children only
Take log₂ of the node count
questions.explanation: Solve: fun depth(n) = if (n == null) 0 else 1 + max(depth(n.left), depth(n.right)). O(n) time, O(h) stack. log₂ of the node count is only right for a perfectly balanced tree.

questions.prompt: Invert a binary tree (mirror it left to right).
options: Swap left and right at every node, recursing into both
Reverse the in-order list of values
Swap only the root's two children
Sort the values in descending order
questions.explanation: Solve: if (n == null) return; swap(n.left, n.right); invert(n.left); invert(n.right). Every node needs its own swap — swapping only at the root leaves each subtree un-mirrored inside.

questions.prompt: Given two binary trees, return whether they are identical in shape and values.
options: Recursively compare the values, then left with left and right with right
Compare their in-order traversals only
Compare their node counts
Compare their root values
questions.explanation: Solve: same(a, b) = both null → true; one null → false; else a.val == b.val && same(a.left, b.left) && same(a.right, b.right). In-order alone cannot tell a left-leaning chain from a right-leaning one with the same values.

questions.prompt: Return the right-side view of a binary tree — the last node you would see on each level.
options: BFS level by level, recording the last node of each level
Follow right children only from the root
Take every second value of the in-order traversal
Return the leaves from left to right
questions.explanation: Solve: queue the root; for each level, pop its size nodes and record the last one. Following right children fails when the left subtree is deeper — its lower nodes are visible from the right too.

questions.prompt: Given a binary tree and a target, return whether some root-to-leaf path adds up to the target.
options: DFS subtracting each value, succeeding at a leaf with remainder 0
Check whether any single node equals the target
Add up every node and compare
BFS adding up each level
questions.explanation: Solve: has(n, t) = n != null && (if leaf: t == n.val else has(n.left, t − n.val) || has(n.right, t − n.val)). Check at a leaf, not at null, or a node with one child would count its missing side as a path.

questions.prompt: Return whether a binary tree is symmetric around its centre.
options: Mirror check: compare left.left with right.right and left.right with right.left
Check that the in-order traversal is a palindrome
Check that both subtrees have the same size
Check that the left and right subtrees are identical
questions.explanation: Solve: mirror(a, b) = both null → true; one null → false; else a.val == b.val && mirror(a.left, b.right) && mirror(a.right, b.left). Identical subtrees are the wrong test — symmetric means mirrored.

questions.prompt: Given a BST and two nodes p and q, return their lowest common ancestor.
options: From the root, go left if both are smaller, right if both are larger, otherwise stop here
Average the two nodes' depths
Always return the root
Return whichever of p and q is smaller
questions.explanation: Solve: the first node whose value lies between p and q (inclusive) splits them, so it is the LCA. O(h) time, O(1) space iteratively. BST order is what lets you skip the general-tree search.

questions.prompt: Return whether a binary tree is height-balanced (subtree heights differ by at most 1 everywhere), in O(n).
options: Post-order returning the height, or −1 as soon as any subtree is unbalanced
Recompute the height from scratch at every node
Compare the root's two subtree heights only
Compare the leftmost and rightmost depths
questions.explanation: Solve: h(n) = null → 0; l = h(left), r = h(right); if l == −1 || r == −1 || |l − r| > 1 return −1; else 1 + max(l, r). One pass. Recomputing heights at every node is O(n²) on a skewed tree; checking only the root misses deeper imbalance.

questions.prompt: Return the diameter of a binary tree — the number of edges on its longest path between any two nodes.
options: At each node try left height + right height; keep the max while returning 1 + max(heights)
Twice the height of the root
The longest path starting at the root
The number of leaves
questions.explanation: Solve: one post-order pass. The longest path bends at some node, and that node may not be the root — a tall left subtree can hold the whole path. Track best = max(best, l + r) and return 1 + max(l, r).

questions.prompt: Convert a sorted array into a height-balanced BST.
options: Make the middle element the root; recurse on the left and right halves
Insert the elements into a BST in order
Make the first element the root, and the rest its right chain
Build a min-heap from the array
questions.explanation: Solve: build(lo, hi) = if lo > hi null else mid = (lo + hi) / 2, node(nums[mid]) with left = build(lo, mid − 1) and right = build(mid + 1, hi). Inserting sorted values one by one makes a linked list of height n.

quiz.title: Picture Round: Read the Diagram
quiz.description: Whiteboard-style questions — look at the array, tree, grid or graph and work out the answer.

questions.prompt: Two pointers on this sorted array, looking for a pair that sums to 9. Right now L + R = 2 + 15 = 17. What happens next?
options: Move R left — the sum is too big
Move L right — the sum is too big
Stop — no pair can exist
Move both pointers inward at once
questions.explanation: Solve: moving L right can only make the sum bigger, so the only useful move is R left. 2 + 11 = 13, still too big, so R moves again: 2 + 7 = 9. The pair is at indices 0 and 1. Each step rules out one element, so the whole search is O(n).

questions.prompt: Insert 5 into this binary search tree. Where does it go?
options: Right child of 4
Left child of 6
Right child of 3
Left child of 10
questions.explanation: Solve: 5 < 8 go left to 3; 5 > 3 go right to 6; 5 < 6 go left to 4; 5 > 4 go right — that slot is empty, so 5 becomes 4's right child. Insertion always ends at an empty slot; the left of 6 and the right of 3 are already taken.

figure.caption: A BST — smaller keys to the left

questions.prompt: Run BFS from A on this graph, visiting neighbours in alphabetical order. What is the visit order?
options: A, B, C, D, E, F
A, B, D, F, E, C
A, C, E, F, D, B
A, B, C, F, D, E
questions.explanation: Solve: queue [A] → visit A, enqueue B, C. Visit B, enqueue D. Visit C, enqueue E. Visit D, enqueue F. Visit E (F is already queued). Visit F. BFS finishes a whole level before going deeper. A, B, D, F, E, C is the DFS order.

questions.prompt: Checking brackets for balance: after reading "{([" the stack looks like this. The next character is ')'. What happens?
options: Invalid — ')' must match the top '[', and it does not
Pop the '(' from the middle of the stack
Push ')' onto the stack
Skip ')' and keep reading
questions.explanation: Solve: a closer can only close the most recent opener — the top of the stack. The top is '[', so ')' fails right away and the string is invalid, whatever follows. A stack cannot reach into its middle, and that is exactly the rule nesting needs.

figure.caption: Open brackets so far, top first

questions.prompt: Merge the overlapping intervals shown on this timeline. What is the result?
questions.explanation: Solve: sort by start. [1, 3] and [2, 6] overlap (2 ≤ 3), so they become [1, 6]. [8, 10] starts after 6, so it stands alone, and so does [15, 18]. Gaps between the blocks stay gaps — merging never fills them.

questions.prompt: 1 is land and 0 is water. Land cells connect up, down, left and right (not diagonally). How many islands are there?
options: 2 — diagonal cells count as touching
9 — one per land cell
questions.explanation: Solve: scan the cells; on each unvisited 1, add one island and flood-fill it. The top-left 2×2 block is one island. The lone 1 in the middle is the second. The L-shape down the right edge is the third. The middle cell only touches that L-shape diagonally, which does not count here.

questions.prompt: Binary search for 11. The first probe, mid, lands on 7. What is the next search range?
options: lo moves to index 4 — search 9, 11, 13
hi moves to index 2 — search 1, 3, 5
lo moves to index 3 — search 7 onwards
Stop — 11 is not at mid
questions.explanation: Solve: 7 < 11, so the target can only be to the right: lo = mid + 1 = 4. The next mid is index 5, which holds 11 — found in 2 probes. Setting lo = mid instead of mid + 1 is the classic bug that loops forever once two elements remain.

questions.prompt: This linked list has a cycle. Floyd's slow and fast pointers both start at node 1. Which node is the cycle's entry?
options: Node 3
Node 5
Node 1
There is no cycle
questions.explanation: Solve: 5 points back to 3, so 3 is the first node visited twice. Floyd finds it in two phases: slow (1 step) and fast (2 steps) meet somewhere inside the loop; then restart one pointer at the head and step both one at a time — they meet at the entry. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.prompt: Move only right or down from S to E. '#' is blocked. How many different paths are there?
questions.explanation: Solve: paths[r][c] = paths from above + paths from the left, and a blocked cell holds 0. The top row and left column have 1 each; the centre is 0; the cell right of centre gets 1 + 0 = 1, the cell below centre 0 + 1 = 1, so E gets 1 + 1 = 2 — around the top, or around the left. Without the block it would be 6.

questions.prompt: Insert 2 into this min-heap. Where does 2 end up?
options: Where 6 was — the root's right child — after one swap
At the root
As a new leaf under 6, with no swaps
As the left child of 3
questions.explanation: Solve: a new value goes into the next free slot — the second child of 6 — then sifts up. 2 < 6, so they swap; 2 > 1, so it stops. The array becomes [1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8, 6]. It never passes 1, because a min-heap only needs each parent ≤ its children.

quiz.title: Story Round: The Food Delivery App
quiz.description: Three stories from a food-delivery startup — orders, routes and shifts — with questions on each.

questions.prompt: Support needs to pull up any order by its id instantly, while the customer waits on the phone. How should Maya store the orders?
options: A hash map from order id to order — O(1) average lookup
A plain list, scanned from the start
A list sorted by restaurant name
A stack with the newest order on top
questions.explanation: Solve: the question is always "give me order #id", which is exactly what a hash map answers in O(1) on average. A scan checks up to 50,000 orders per call; sorting by restaurant does not help a lookup by id; a stack can only show its top.

story.title: QuickBite · The lunch rush
story.text: Maya is the first engineer at QuickBite, a food-delivery startup. Every order has an id, a restaurant and the minute it was placed. At lunch the app takes 50,000 orders, and three teams come to Maya with requests.

questions.prompt: Each kitchen must see its orders in exactly the order they were placed, and remove each one when it is cooked. Which structure?
options: A queue per kitchen — first in, first out
A stack per kitchen — newest first
A hash set of order ids
A max-heap keyed by order value
questions.explanation: Solve: new orders join the back; the cook takes from the front. Both are O(1), and the oldest order is always served first — which is what "in the order they were placed" means. A stack would make the first customer wait for everyone after them.

story.title: QuickBite · The lunch rush
story.text: Maya is the first engineer at QuickBite, a food-delivery startup. Every order has an id, a restaurant and the minute it was placed. At lunch the app takes 50,000 orders, and three teams come to Maya with requests.

questions.prompt: Finance keeps asking how many orders arrived between two minutes. From the figure, how many arrived from 12:01 to 12:03 inclusive — and how should Maya answer thousands of these questions?
options: 116 — build prefix sums once; each question is one subtraction
71 — adding only the two end minutes
153 — adding 12:01 to the end
questions.explanation: Solve: 30 + 45 + 41 = 116. With prefix = [0, 12, 42, 87, 128, 156, 165], minutes 1 to 3 are prefix[4] − prefix[1] = 128 − 12 = 116. Building it once is O(n), and every later question is O(1) instead of re-adding the range.

story.title: QuickBite · The lunch rush
story.text: Maya is the first engineer at QuickBite, a food-delivery startup. Every order has an id, a restaurant and the minute it was placed. At lunch the app takes 50,000 orders, and three teams come to Maya with requests.

questions.prompt: At the end of the day, Maya must show the 3 restaurants with the most orders, out of 2,000 restaurants. Best approach?
options: Count orders per restaurant in a hash map, then keep a size-3 min-heap
Sort all 50,000 orders by time
Show the 3 restaurants that got the earliest orders
Binary search the list of orders
questions.explanation: Solve: one pass fills counts[restaurant]++. Then push each (restaurant, count) onto a min-heap and pop when it holds more than 3. The heap's root is the weakest of the current top 3. O(n + r log 3). Sorting orders by time says nothing about how many each restaurant got.

story.title: QuickBite · The lunch rush
story.text: Maya is the first engineer at QuickBite, a food-delivery startup. Every order has an id, a restaurant and the minute it was placed. At lunch the app takes 50,000 orders, and three teams come to Maya with requests.

questions.prompt: What is Sam's fastest route from R to C?
options: 6 minutes, via R–Y–X–Z–C
7 minutes, via R–X–Z–C
8 minutes, via R–Y–X–C
9 minutes, via R–X–C
questions.explanation: Solve with Dijkstra from R: Y = 2, then X = min(4, 2 + 1) = 3, then Z = min(2 + 7, 3 + 2) = 5, then C = min(3 + 5, 5 + 1) = 6. The route with the fewest streets (R–X–C) is the slowest of the four.

story.title: QuickBite · Getting the food there
story.text: Rider Sam picks up at restaurant R and delivers to a customer at C. The map shows the streets between them, each labelled with the minutes it takes to ride.

questions.prompt: A bug makes the app count streets instead of minutes. Which route would it pick, and why is that wrong here?
options: R–X–C, just 2 streets — BFS ignores minutes, so Sam rides 9 minutes instead of 6
R–Y–X–Z–C — BFS always finds the fastest route
R–Y–Z–C, 3 streets — it is the first route BFS reaches
None — BFS cannot run on a street map
questions.explanation: Solve: BFS finds the fewest edges, which here is R–X–C with 2 streets. That is only the fastest route when every street takes the same time. With weights, use Dijkstra — the 4-street route wins at 6 minutes.

story.title: QuickBite · Getting the food there
story.text: Rider Sam picks up at restaurant R and delivers to a customer at C. The map shows the streets between them, each labelled with the minutes it takes to ride.

questions.prompt: The street between X and Z closes for repairs. What is the fastest route now?
options: 8 minutes, via R–Y–X–C
6 minutes — nothing changes
9 minutes, via R–X–C
10 minutes, via R–Y–Z–C
questions.explanation: Solve: without X–Z, Z can only be reached from Y (2 + 7 = 9), so C through Z costs 10. C through X costs 3 + 5 = 8. Remove the edge and run Dijkstra again: 8 via R–Y–X–C.

story.title: QuickBite · Getting the food there
story.text: Rider Sam picks up at restaurant R and delivers to a customer at C. The map shows the streets between them, each labelled with the minutes it takes to ride.

questions.prompt: What is the largest number of riders on duty at the same time?
options: 5 — one for each rider
questions.explanation: Solve: sweep through the day, adding one at each shift start and removing one at each end. From 12:00 to 14:00 Ana, Ben and Cal all work — 3. No other moment has more than 2.

figure.caption: Rider shifts, hour of the day

story.title: QuickBite · Tomorrow's rider shifts
story.text: Priya plans tomorrow's rider shifts on a 24-hour clock. Customers can order from 8:00 to 22:00, and the timeline shows each rider's shift.

questions.prompt: Is there any time between 8:00 and 22:00 when no rider is on duty?
options: Yes — from 18:00 to 19:00
No — the shifts cover the whole day
Yes — from 14:00 to 16:00
Yes — from 17:00 to 18:00
questions.explanation: Solve: sort by start and merge. 8–14, 11–17 and 12–15 merge into 8–17; 16–18 overlaps, giving 8–18. Dev starts at 19, so 18:00–19:00 has nobody. From 14 to 16 Ben is still working, and from 17 to 18 Eve is.

figure.caption: Rider shifts, hour of the day

story.title: QuickBite · Tomorrow's rider shifts
story.text: Priya plans tomorrow's rider shifts on a 24-hour clock. Customers can order from 8:00 to 22:00, and the timeline shows each rider's shift.

questions.prompt: Priya wants the app to reject any new shift that overlaps one the same rider already has. Riders can have many shifts. What should the check do?
options: Keep each rider's shifts sorted by start; the new one fits if it ends before the next shift starts and starts after the previous one ends
Compare it only with the rider's first shift
Check that the rider's total hours stay under 24
Check that no other rider works at that time
questions.explanation: Solve: existing shifts never overlap each other, so only the two neighbours of the new start time can clash. With a sorted structure (a TreeMap of start → end), find them in O(log n) and check prev.end ≤ start and end ≤ next.start. Other riders are irrelevant — they are different people.
