quiz.title: Advanced Graphs Round
quiz.description: Weighted paths, cycles, components and spanning trees — pick the algorithm the graph calls for.

questions.prompt: Single-source shortest paths when every edge weight is non-negative:
options: Dijkstra with a min-heap — O((V + E) log V)
Plain BFS — O(V + E)
DFS, keeping the smallest sum seen per node
Bellman-Ford — the only correct choice once edges have weights
questions.explanation: Non-negative weights mean the closest unsettled node can never get closer later, so Dijkstra settles each node once. BFS is only right when all weights are equal; Bellman-Ford is correct but O(V·E).

questions.prompt: The graph has negative edge weights and you must report a negative cycle if one exists:
options: Bellman-Ford — if a V-th round still relaxes an edge, a negative cycle exists
Dijkstra — it re-visits nodes when a weight is negative
Topological sort
Prim's algorithm
questions.explanation: Any shortest path uses at most V − 1 edges, so V − 1 rounds of relaxing every edge settle all distances. If round V still improves something, a cycle keeps lowering the cost. Dijkstra can return wrong answers with negative edges.

questions.prompt: Every edge weighs either 0 or 1. The fastest shortest-path approach:
options: 0-1 BFS with a deque — push 0-edges to the front, 1-edges to the back — O(V + E)
Dijkstra is required — O(E log V)
Plain BFS that ignores the weights
Floyd-Warshall — O(V³)
questions.explanation: A 0-edge keeps the same distance, so it goes to the front; a 1-edge adds one, so it goes to the back. The deque stays sorted by distance without a heap. Dijkstra also works, but it is not required and is a log factor slower.

questions.prompt: Scenario: n courses with prerequisite pairs (a needs b). Can a student finish them all?
options: Kahn's topological sort — if fewer than n courses are dequeued, there is a cycle
BFS from course 0 and check that every course is reached
Union-find over the prerequisite pairs
Sort courses by their number of prerequisites
questions.explanation: Solve: build edges b → a and count in-degrees. Queue every course with in-degree 0; pop one, decrement its neighbours, and queue any that reach 0. If all n come out, an order exists. Union-find ignores direction, so it cannot tell a cycle from a diamond.

figure.caption: Prerequisites (b → a: take b before a)

questions.prompt: Scenario: friendships are added live, and users keep asking "are A and B in the same friend group?" Best structure:
options: Union-find with path compression and union by rank — nearly O(1) per operation
A fresh BFS from A for every question
Floyd-Warshall, re-run after every new friendship
Each friend list kept in a sorted array
questions.explanation: Solve: a new friendship calls union(a, b); a question checks find(a) == find(b). With both optimisations each call is O(α(n)) — effectively constant. BFS per question is O(V + E) every time.

questions.prompt: Scenario: lay fibre so every office is connected, using the least total cable. Possible links and their lengths are known:
options: Kruskal: sort links by length, keep each one that does not close a cycle
Dijkstra from headquarters
Connect each office to its nearest neighbour only
Topologically sort the offices
questions.explanation: Solve: this is a minimum spanning tree. Take links shortest first; union-find tells you whether the two offices are already connected, in which case you skip the link. Stop at V − 1 links. Dijkstra minimises each office's distance to HQ, not the total cable; nearest-neighbour can leave separate islands.

questions.prompt: Can a graph's nodes be split into two groups with every edge crossing between them (bipartite)?
options: BFS/DFS two-colouring — fail if an edge joins two same-coloured nodes
Yes whenever the number of nodes is even
Yes whenever every node has even degree
Only if the graph has no cycles at all
questions.explanation: Colour a start node 0 and each neighbour the opposite colour. A conflict means an odd cycle, and a graph is bipartite exactly when it has none. Even cycles are fine — a square is bipartite.

questions.prompt: Find the strongly connected components of a directed graph:
options: Tarjan's or Kosaraju's algorithm — O(V + E)
Union-find over the directed edges
Dijkstra from every node
A single BFS from any node
questions.explanation: A strongly connected component needs paths both ways. Kosaraju runs DFS twice (the second time on the reversed graph); Tarjan does it in one DFS with low-link values. Union-find treats edges as two-way, so it would merge nodes that only reach one direction.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a wildfire map grid; several cells are burning, and fire spreads to neighbours each minute. When is the last cell reached?
options: Multi-source BFS — enqueue every fire at minute 0 and expand level by level
A separate BFS from each fire, keeping the minimum per cell
DFS from the first fire only
Dijkstra with random edge weights
questions.explanation: Solve: put all burning cells in the queue together, then run BFS; each level is one minute. The last level reached is the answer (or −1 if some cell is never reached). One BFS per fire gives the same answer at k times the cost.

questions.prompt: Scenario: cheapest flight from A to B with at most k stops:
options: Bellman-Ford limited to k + 1 rounds, relaxing from the previous round's costs
Plain Dijkstra on price, ignoring the stop count
Greedy: always take the cheapest outgoing flight
Topological sort of the airports
questions.explanation: Solve: round r allows r flights. Each round copies the cost array and relaxes every flight using only last round's costs, so a path never gains two flights in one round. After k + 1 rounds read cost[B]. Plain Dijkstra may lock in a cheap route that has too many stops.

quiz.title: Advanced DP Round
quiz.description: State design, recurrences and the counterexamples that break greedy.

questions.prompt: Scenario: rob houses along a street for the most money, but never two neighbouring houses. Recurrence:
options: best[i] = max(best[i − 1], best[i − 2] + value[i])
best[i] = best[i − 1] + value[i]
Take every house at an even index
Take the richest house, skip its neighbours, repeat
questions.explanation: Solve: at house i you either skip it (best[i − 1]) or rob it on top of best[i − 2]. Two variables are enough — O(n) time, O(1) space. Greedy fails on [2, 3, 2]: it takes 3, but 2 + 2 = 4.

questions.prompt: Longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n):
options: Keep a tails array and binary-search where each value belongs
Sort the array and take the longest run
Compare all pairs — the O(n²) DP is already O(n log n)
Greedy: extend whenever the next value is larger
questions.explanation: tails[k] holds the smallest possible ending of an increasing run of length k + 1. Each value replaces the first tail ≥ it, or extends the array. The array's length is the answer. Greedy fails on [3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 6].

questions.prompt: Edit distance (insert / delete / replace) between strings a and b — the recurrence:
options: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] if the characters match, else 1 + min(insert, delete, replace)
dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1]
Count the positions where the characters differ
The difference between the two lengths
questions.explanation: dp[i][j] is the cost to turn a's first i characters into b's first j. The three neighbours are delete (dp[i−1][j]), insert (dp[i][j−1]) and replace (dp[i−1][j−1]). Counting position-wise differences fails on "abc" → "xabc": every position differs, but one insert fixes it.

questions.prompt: 0/1 knapsack with a single 1-D array dp[capacity]. The inner loop over capacity must go:
options: From high to low, so each item is counted at most once
From low to high — that is what enforces the 0/1 rule
In any order — the result is the same
After sorting the items by value
questions.explanation: dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c − w] + v) must read dp[c − w] from before this item. Going downward keeps it untouched. Going upward may read a value that already includes the item, which is the unbounded knapsack.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a courier must visit 15 stops once each and return, with the shortest route. Exact approach:
options: Bitmask DP over (visited set, current stop) — about 2ⁿ · n² ≈ 7 × 10⁶ steps
Try every order — 15! ≈ 1.3 × 10¹²
Greedy nearest-neighbour — it is exact
Dijkstra from the depot
questions.explanation: Solve: dp[mask][v] = shortest path that visits exactly the stops in mask and ends at v. Extend with dp[mask | 1 << u][u] = min(…, dp[mask][v] + dist[v][u]). Answer = min over v of dp[all][v] + dist[v][depot]. The bitmask turns n! orders into 2ⁿ sets.

questions.prompt: Scenario: stock trading with unlimited trades, but after selling you must wait one day before buying. Best approach:
options: State machine DP — track hold / just-sold / resting profit day by day
Buy at the global minimum, sell at the global maximum
Add up every positive day-to-day price increase
Binary search for the best buy day
questions.explanation: Solve: hold = max(hold, rest − price); sold = hold + price; rest = max(rest, sold) — each using the previous day's values. Answer = max(sold, rest). Adding every rise is right without a cooldown, but here it can buy the day after a sale.

questions.prompt: Burst balloons for coins, where each burst scores the product of its current neighbours. The key DP idea:
options: Interval DP — pick which balloon in (i, j) bursts last
Greedy — always burst the smallest balloon first
Sort the balloons and pair up neighbours
Try every order with backtracking and no memo
questions.explanation: If k is the last to burst inside (i, j), its neighbours at that moment are exactly i and j, so dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + v[i]·v[k]·v[j]. Thinking "first" instead of "last" leaves the two sides dependent on each other. O(n³).

questions.prompt: Scenario: invite employees to a party for the most total fun, but never an employee together with their direct manager. The org chart is a tree:
options: Tree DP — each person returns (best if invited, best if not)
Invite every other level of the org chart
Invite the most fun person, remove their neighbours, repeat
BFS and invite only the leaves
questions.explanation: Solve: post-order. in(v) = fun(v) + Σ out(child); out(v) = Σ max(in(child), out(child)). Answer = max(in(root), out(root)). O(n). Alternating levels fails when two consecutive levels are both worth skipping.

figure.caption: Org chart with fun scores (parent = manager)

questions.prompt: Can "cars" be split into words from the dictionary {"car", "ca", "rs"}?
options: Yes — dp[i] is true if some word ends at i and dp[start of that word] is true
No — greedily taking the longest word "car" leaves an unmatched "s"
Yes — every dictionary word appears somewhere in the string
No — the dictionary has no word starting with 's'
questions.explanation: Solve: dp[0] = true; dp[2] ("ca") = true; dp[3] ("car") = true; dp[4] = dp[2] && "rs" is a word = true. Split: "ca" + "rs". Greedy commits to "car" and fails. O(n²) substring checks with a hash set of words.

questions.prompt: Letters map to numbers (A = 1 … Z = 26). How many ways can "226" be decoded?
options: 3 — dp[i] = dp[i − 1] if the last digit is 1–9, plus dp[i − 2] if the last two form 10–26
2 — one per split point
1 — digits decode one at a time
questions.explanation: Solve: "2 2 6" (BBF), "22 6" (VF), "2 26" (BZ) = 3. A '0' can only be used as part of 10 or 20, which is what the digit checks handle — "06" is not a valid code. O(n) time with two variables.

quiz.title: Advanced Data Structures Round
quiz.description: Range queries, time-indexed stores, schedulers and O(1) designs — the structures behind the fast answer.

questions.prompt: Design a time-based key-value store: set(key, value, t) with increasing t, and get(key, t) returning the value set at the latest time ≤ t.
options: Per key, append (t, value) to a list and binary search it by t — O(log n) get
A hash map holding only the latest value per key
Scan every stored entry on each get
Sort the whole store on every get
questions.explanation: Solve: map key → list of (t, value). Timestamps only increase, so each list is already sorted and set is an O(1) append. get binary-searches for the last t' ≤ t and returns "" if there is none. Keeping only the latest value cannot answer a question about the past.

questions.prompt: Many interleaved "add x to index i" updates and "sum of range [l, r]" queries:
options: A Fenwick tree or segment tree — O(log n) for both
Prefix sums — O(1) queries and O(1) updates
A running total — O(1) for both
A sorted array with binary search
questions.explanation: Prefix sums give O(1) queries, but one update shifts every later prefix — O(n). A Fenwick tree stores partial sums over power-of-two blocks, so both operations touch O(log n) cells.

questions.prompt: Tasks [A, A, A, B, B, B] must run with at least n = 2 idle slots between identical tasks. What is the fewest time slots needed?
options: 8 — (maxCount − 1) × (n + 1) + number of tasks with maxCount = 2 × 3 + 2
6 — one slot per task
7 — tasks plus one idle
9 — every slot after a task sits idle
questions.explanation: Solve: the most frequent task makes the frame: A _ _ A _ _ A. B fills a gap in each frame and ties at the end: A B _ A B _ A B = 8. The answer is the larger of that formula and the task count, since with enough variety there are no idles at all.

questions.prompt: Design a set with insert, remove and getRandom, all in O(1) on average.
options: An array of values plus a map of value → index; remove swaps the value with the last one, then pops
A hash set only — picking a random element is O(1)
A linked list, walking to a random index
A sorted array
questions.explanation: Solve: insert appends and records the index. remove(x) moves the last element into x's slot, updates its index, and pops the end. getRandom picks arr[random(size)]. Hash sets have no index access, so a uniform random pick means iterating.

questions.prompt: Return the k-th smallest value in a BST.
options: In-order traversal, stopping at the k-th node visited — O(h + k)
Level-order traversal, taking the k-th node
Walk left k times from the root
Collect all the values, then sort them
questions.explanation: Solve: an iterative in-order with a stack: push left children, pop, count, and stop when the count reaches k. The BST already gives sorted order, so sorting is wasted work. Level order is not sorted.

questions.prompt: For every element, find the next element to its right that is larger:
options: A monotonic stack — each index is pushed and popped once, O(n)
Nested loops with an early break — O(n) overall
Sort the array, then look each value up in a hash map
Binary search on the right-hand side
questions.explanation: Keep indices whose answer is still unknown on a stack of decreasing values. A new value pops every smaller one — it is their answer — and then pushes itself. An early break still costs O(n²) on a decreasing array.

questions.prompt: Scenario: block a billion known malicious URLs using little memory. An occasional false alarm is fine; missing a bad URL is not:
options: A Bloom filter — no false negatives, tunable false-positive rate
A hash set of every URL
A sorted list on disk with binary search
A count-min sketch for exact membership
questions.explanation: Solve: set k bit positions per URL. A lookup with any bit clear is definitely safe; all bits set means "probably bad", so confirm against the slow exact store. About 10 bits per URL gives roughly 1% false positives — around 1.2 GB instead of tens of GB.

questions.prompt: A static array with a million range-minimum queries. Fastest per query:
options: A sparse table — O(n log n) to build, O(1) per query
A Fenwick tree — O(1) per query
Prefix minimums — any range in O(1)
Rescan each range — O(1) amortised
questions.explanation: The minimum is fine with overlap, so any range is covered by two power-of-two blocks: min(st[k][l], st[k][r − 2ᵏ + 1]). Prefix minimums only answer ranges that start at index 0.

questions.prompt: When is a balanced BST (TreeMap) the better choice over a hash map?
options: When you need ordered queries — floor, ceiling, range scans — in O(log n)
When you need the fastest average exact-key lookup
When the keys cannot be compared
When the structure must use O(1) memory
questions.explanation: Hash maps win exact lookups at O(1) average but know nothing about order. A balanced BST answers "the largest key ≤ x" or "every key between a and b" directly — which is what schedules, price books and time series need.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a game leaderboard with frequent score updates and "what is my rank?" queries. Scores are integers from 0 to 1,000,000:
options: A Fenwick tree over score counts — rank = number of higher scores + 1, O(log S)
Re-sort the whole board on every update
A hash map of player → score, scanning it for each rank
A queue of players in join order
questions.explanation: Solve: count[s] = players with score s, stored in a Fenwick tree. An update is add(old, −1) then add(new, +1); rank = (total − prefix(score)) + 1. Keep player → score in a map for the old value. Both operations are O(log 10⁶) ≈ 20 steps.

quiz.title: Scenario Round: Real Systems
quiz.description: Product problems — rate limits, logs, trends, calendars — solved with the right algorithm.

questions.prompt: Scenario: allow each user at most 100 API requests in any rolling 60-second window:
options: Per user, a queue of timestamps — drop those older than 60 s, reject if 100 remain
One global counter reset once a day
Sort every request by user once a minute
A stack of timestamps per user, popped from the top
questions.explanation: Solve: on each request, pop from the front while front ≤ now − 60 s. If size < 100, push now and allow; otherwise reject. Each timestamp is pushed and popped once. The oldest entries leave first, so it is a queue, not a stack. A token bucket gives a similar limit in O(1) memory.

questions.prompt: Scenario: merge k log files, each already sorted by timestamp, N lines in total:
options: A k-way merge with a min-heap of each file's next line — O(N log k)
Concatenate everything and sort — O(N log N)
Merge file 1 with 2, then the result with 3, and so on — O(N·k)
Take one line from each file in turn
questions.explanation: Solve: push the first line of every file onto a heap keyed by timestamp. Pop the smallest, write it, and push the next line from the same file. The heap never holds more than k lines, so it streams files too big for memory.

questions.prompt: Scenario: show the top 10 trending hashtags from millions of posts:
options: Count in a hash map, then keep a size-10 min-heap — O(n log 10)
Re-sort every hashtag by count after each post
Push every tag onto a max-heap and pop 10
Show the 10 most recent hashtags
questions.explanation: Solve: count[tag]++ per post. Then for each (tag, count): push onto a min-heap and pop whenever its size passes 10. The heap's root is the weakest of the current top 10, so anything smaller is dropped at once. A max-heap of every tag works but costs O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Scenario: given today's meetings as (start, end), how many rooms does the office need?
options: Sort by start; a min-heap of end times — its peak size is the answer
Divide the number of meetings by 8 working hours
Sort by duration and pack meetings greedily
Count the meetings that overlap the first one
questions.explanation: Solve: for each meeting in start order, pop the heap's top if that meeting has ended (end ≤ start) — its room is free — then push this meeting's end. The largest heap size is the room count. A line sweep over +1/−1 events gives the same answer.

questions.prompt: Scenario: pick 1,000 records uniformly at random from a stream of unknown length, in one pass and O(1,000) memory:
options: Reservoir sampling — keep record i with probability 1,000 / i
Keep the first 1,000 records
Keep every 1,000th record
Store the whole stream, then shuffle it
questions.explanation: Solve: fill the reservoir with the first 1,000. For record i > 1,000, pick j in [1, i]; if j ≤ 1,000, replace slot j. Every record ends up with an equal 1,000 / n chance. Storing everything breaks the memory limit; the other two are biased.

questions.prompt: Scenario: find every 10-letter DNA sequence that occurs more than once in a genome of n letters:
options: A rolling hash over each 10-letter window, with a set of seen hashes — O(n)
Compare every pair of windows — O(n²)
Sort the genome's letters
Run KMP with an empty pattern
questions.explanation: Solve: with 4 letters, each window packs into 20 bits: h = ((h << 2) | code(c)) & 0xFFFFF. Add h to seen; if already present, add it to repeated. Each slide is O(1), and this packing is collision-free, so no string comparison is needed.

questions.prompt: Scenario: ship packages in their given order within D days. What is the smallest daily truck capacity that works?
options: Binary search on the capacity, greedily checking whether D days suffice
Try every capacity from 1 upward
Total weight ÷ D, rounded up
Sort the packages and ship the heaviest first
questions.explanation: Solve: lo = heaviest package, hi = total weight. For mid, fill each day until the next package would overflow, then start a new day. If that takes ≤ D days, try smaller (hi = mid); otherwise lo = mid + 1. Feasibility only flips once, which is what makes binary search valid. Total ÷ D ignores that packages cannot be split.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a calendar app must reject a new event that overlaps an existing one, with thousands of events:
options: A balanced BST keyed by start — check only the floor and ceiling neighbours, O(log n)
Scan every event on each insert
A hash map keyed by start time
A stack of events in creation order
questions.explanation: Solve: prev = floorEntry(start), next = ceilingEntry(start). The event fits if prev.end ≤ start and end ≤ next.start. Existing events never overlap each other, so only those two neighbours can clash. A hash map cannot find neighbouring times.

questions.prompt: Scenario: from a pile of airline tickets (from, to), rebuild the one itinerary that uses every ticket exactly once:
options: Hierholzer's algorithm — DFS that uses up edges and adds airports on the way back
Sort tickets by departure airport and chain them greedily
BFS from the starting airport
Topologically sort the airports
questions.explanation: Solve: every ticket is an edge, used once — an Eulerian path. Walk DFS, removing each ticket as you use it; when an airport has none left, prepend it to the answer. Greedy chaining can walk into a dead end early; topological sort fails because routes revisit airports.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a warehouse robot needs the shortest path across a grid with shelves, and should explore as few cells as possible:
options: A* with Manhattan distance as the heuristic
DFS until it happens to reach the goal
Dijkstra with a negative heuristic added
Greedy best-first search — it is always optimal
questions.explanation: Solve: expand by f = g (steps so far) + h (Manhattan distance to the goal). With 4-way moves, Manhattan never overestimates, so A* stays optimal while skipping cells that head away from the goal. Greedy best-first uses h alone and can return a longer path.

quiz.title: Scenario Round: Constraints & Trade-offs
quiz.description: Read the limits first — n, memory, accuracy — and let them pick the algorithm.

questions.prompt: The problem says n ≤ 20 and asks for the best subset of items. What do the limits allow?
options: Enumerating every subset — 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶ with a bitmask is fine
Only an O(n log n) solution will pass
Only O(n) will pass
Backtracking over 20 items is always too slow
questions.explanation: A tiny n is a hint: the intended solution is exponential. Loop mask from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1; bit i set means item i is taken. At about 20 · 10⁶ operations it runs well under a second.

questions.prompt: Subset sum with n = 40 items whose values reach 10⁹:
options: Meet in the middle — enumerate both halves (2 × 2²⁰), sort one, binary-search it
Enumerate all 2⁴⁰ ≈ 10¹² subsets
Greedy: take the largest items first
DP over every possible sum up to 4 × 10¹⁰
questions.explanation: Split into two halves of 20 and list each half's subset sums — about 10⁶ each. Sort one list; for each sum s in the other, binary-search for target − s. Huge values rule out sum-indexed DP, and 2⁴⁰ is too slow.

questions.prompt: n = 10⁵ and the problem involves pairs of elements. What complexity do you aim for?
options: O(n log n) or better — O(n²) is 10¹⁰ operations
O(n²) is fine for 10⁵
O(n³) with pruning
O(2ⁿ) with memoisation
questions.explanation: Rough limits for about a second: n ≤ 20 → exponential, ≤ 500 → n³, ≤ 5,000 → n², ≤ 10⁶ → n log n. At 10⁵, all-pairs is out, so reach for sorting, hashing, two pointers or a heap.

questions.prompt: Scenario: 10⁵ hotel bookings each add +1 guest to every day in [l, r], across 10⁵ days. You need the final count per day:
options: A difference array: +1 at l, −1 at r + 1, then one prefix-sum pass — O(n + q)
Loop over each booking's days and add — O(n·q) is fine
A segment tree is required
Sort the bookings by length
questions.explanation: Solve: diff[l] += 1 and diff[r + 1] −= 1 per booking, then count[d] = count[d − 1] + diff[d]. 2 × 10⁵ operations instead of up to 10¹⁰. A lazy segment tree also works, but it is only needed when queries arrive between updates.

questions.prompt: Scenario: count the subarrays that sum to exactly k, where values can be negative:
options: Prefix sums with a hash map of prefix counts — O(n)
A sliding window that shrinks whenever the sum exceeds k
Sort the array, then use two pointers
Binary search over the prefix sums
questions.explanation: Solve: seen = {0: 1}. For each running sum s, add seen[s − k] to the answer, then seen[s]++. A sliding window needs sums that only grow as it widens; negatives break that. Sorting destroys contiguity.

questions.prompt: Scenario: sort a 1 GB file of integers on a machine with 100 MB of RAM:
options: External merge sort — sort 100 MB chunks to disk, then k-way merge them
Load the whole file and quicksort it
Counting sort over the full 32-bit range in memory
Bubble sort directly on disk
questions.explanation: Solve: read about 10 chunks that fit in RAM, sort each and write it out. Then merge all 10 with a min-heap, reading and writing buffered blocks — the disk is read sequentially twice. A 32-bit count array needs 16 GB.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a map has 10⁵ points. Find the two closest ones.
options: Divide and conquer by x, then check a narrow strip around the split — O(n log n)
Compare every pair — about 5 × 10⁹ comparisons
Sort by x and compare neighbours only
Take the two points closest to the origin
questions.explanation: Solve: split by median x, recurse on both halves to get δ, then check only points within δ of the split line, sorted by y — each needs at most about 7 comparisons. Neighbours in x order can be far apart in y, so comparing only neighbours misses pairs.

questions.prompt: Scenario: count the distinct users across billions of events. ±2% is acceptable, and memory must stay in kilobytes:
options: A HyperLogLog-style cardinality sketch
An exact hash set of every user id
Sort every event by user id
A Bloom filter, which counts distinct items exactly
questions.explanation: Solve: hash each id and track, per bucket, the longest run of leading zeros seen; rare long runs mean many distinct values. About 1.5 KB gives roughly 2% error at any scale. An exact set of a billion ids needs gigabytes. A Bloom filter answers membership, not counts.

questions.prompt: Scenario: your recursive DFS crashes with a stack overflow on a path-shaped graph of 10⁶ nodes. The fix:
options: Rewrite it as an iterative DFS with an explicit stack
Add memoisation — that removes the depth
Rely on tail-call optimisation, which every language performs
Sort the nodes before the DFS
questions.explanation: Solve: push the start node onto a heap-allocated stack; loop pop → visit → push unvisited neighbours. The depth now lives in heap memory, not the call stack of about 1 MB. Memoisation cuts repeated work, not depth, and the JVM does not eliminate tail calls.

questions.prompt: Scenario: your O(n²) brute force works and the interviewer asks, "Can you do better?" The strongest next move:
options: Name what the inner loop recomputes, then precompute it — a hash map, prefix sums or sorted order
Offer to rewrite it in a faster language
Add early returns inside the inner loop
Split the work across several threads
questions.explanation: Solve: say it out loud — "for each i, the inner loop searches for x". Then ask which structure answers that search in O(1) or O(log n): a set for existence, a map for counts or indices, prefix sums for ranges, sorting for order. Languages, threads and early exits only change constants.

quiz.title: Coding Round: Trees & Graphs
quiz.description: LCA, serialisation, word ladders, alien alphabets and spanning trees.

questions.prompt: Given a binary tree (not a BST) and nodes p and q, return their lowest common ancestor.
options: Recurse: return the node if it is p or q; if both sides return non-null, this node is the LCA
Use BST ordering to decide which way to go
Return the parent of the deeper node
BFS and return the first level containing both
questions.explanation: Solve: lca(n) = if n == null || n == p || n == q return n; l = lca(n.left); r = lca(n.right); return if (l != null && r != null) n else l ?: r. O(n). There is no ordering to exploit, so both sides must be searched.

questions.prompt: Design serialize and deserialize for a binary tree, so that the string rebuilds the exact tree.
options: Pre-order with a marker for every null child
In-order values only
Level-order values with the nulls left out
The node count followed by the sorted values
questions.explanation: Solve: serialize: visit node, write val or "#", recurse left then right. Deserialize: read tokens in the same order; "#" returns null, otherwise build a node and recurse left, then right. Null markers are what pin the shape — without them many trees share one string.

questions.prompt: Rebuild a binary tree from its pre-order and in-order traversals (values are unique).
options: Pre-order's next value is the root; its index in in-order splits the left and right subtrees
Insert the pre-order values into a BST
In-order's first value is the root
It cannot be done without the post-order too
questions.explanation: Solve: keep a value → index map for in-order and a moving pointer into pre-order. build(lo, hi): root = pre[p++]; m = idx[root]; left = build(lo, m − 1); right = build(m + 1, hi). Build left first, because pre-order lists it first. O(n).

questions.prompt: Return the maximum path sum in a binary tree, where a path can start and end at any nodes.
options: Post-order: each node returns val + max(0, best child gain); update the answer with val + both gains
Add up every positive node
The largest root-to-leaf sum
The largest single value times the height
questions.explanation: Solve: gain(n) = null → 0; l = max(0, gain(left)), r = max(0, gain(right)); best = max(best, n.val + l + r); return n.val + max(l, r). Returning only one side keeps the path unbranched for the parent; max(0, …) drops negative branches. Start best at the minimum value, since all values may be negative.

questions.prompt: A height grid borders the Pacific (top/left) and the Atlantic (bottom/right). Water flows to equal or lower neighbours. Return the cells that can reach both oceans.
options: BFS/DFS inward from each ocean's border going uphill; return the cells both searches reach
DFS downhill from every cell separately
Return the cells taller than all their neighbours
Return the border cells
questions.explanation: Solve: reverse the flow — from the Pacific border, move to neighbours with height ≥ the current one, marking pac[][]; do the same for atl[][]. The answer is where both are true. Two searches, O(m·n), instead of one search per cell, O((m·n)²).

questions.prompt: Word ladder: turn "hit" into "cog" one letter at a time, where every step must be a dictionary word. Return the fewest steps.
options: BFS over words, making neighbours by changing one letter at a time
DFS, returning the first path found
Dijkstra with letter-distance weights
Sort the dictionary and walk it alphabetically
questions.explanation: Solve: queue "hit" at step 1. For each word, try all 26 letters in every position; any unvisited dictionary word goes into the queue at step + 1. The first time "cog" appears is the answer: hit→hot→dot→dog→cog = 5 words. Every step costs the same, so BFS finds the shortest; DFS finds some path.

questions.prompt: Given words sorted in an unknown alien alphabet, return an order of its letters.
options: Compare adjacent words; the first differing letters give an edge — then topological sort
Sort the letters by frequency
Use the first word's letters in order
Union-find the letters that appear together
questions.explanation: Solve: for each adjacent pair, the first position where they differ gives an edge a → b; then run Kahn's algorithm over every letter. A cycle means no valid order. So does a longer word listed before its own prefix ("abc" before "ab") — check that explicitly.

questions.prompt: Given n nodes and a list of undirected edges, return whether they form a valid tree.
options: Exactly n − 1 edges and no cycle (union-find never joins two already-connected nodes)
No node has degree greater than 2
The number of edges equals n
Every node has at least one edge
questions.explanation: Solve: if edges.size != n − 1 return false; then union each edge, failing if find(a) == find(b). n − 1 edges with no cycle forces the graph to be connected. The degree test describes a path, not a tree.

questions.prompt: Given n points, return the minimum total Manhattan distance needed to connect all of them.
options: Prim's algorithm (an O(n²) array version suits the complete graph)
Connect the points in order of x
Dijkstra from point 0
Add up each point's distance to its nearest neighbour
questions.explanation: Solve: every pair is an edge, so E = n². Array Prim keeps dist[] to the growing tree: pick the closest unused point, add its distance, then relax every other point. O(n²) with no heap and no edge list. Nearest-neighbour sums can leave the points in separate clusters.

questions.prompt: Network delay: a signal leaves node k along weighted directed edges. Return the time until every node has received it, or −1.
options: Dijkstra from k; the answer is the largest distance, or −1 if any node is unreachable
BFS counting edges
The sum of all the edge weights
The smallest distance to any node
questions.explanation: Solve: every node receives the signal at its shortest-path time, so the network is done when the farthest node gets it: max(dist). Weights differ, so edge counts from BFS are the wrong measure.

quiz.title: Coding Round: DP & Backtracking
quiz.description: Grid paths, partitions, combinations, regex matching and palindrome cuts.

questions.prompt: A robot moves only right or down on an m × n grid. How many paths go from the top-left to the bottom-right of a 3 × 7 grid?
options: 28 — paths[r][c] = paths[r − 1][c] + paths[r][c − 1]
questions.explanation: Solve: the first row and column have one path each; every other cell adds the cell above and the cell to its left. Equivalently C(m + n − 2, m − 1) = C(8, 2) = 28. One row of DP is enough: O(n) space.

questions.prompt: nums[i] is the maximum jump from index i. Return whether you can reach the last index.
options: Greedy: track the farthest reachable index; fail if i ever passes it
BFS over every possible jump is required
Always take the largest jump available
Succeed exactly when no value is zero
questions.explanation: Solve: far = 0; for i in indices: if i > far return false; far = max(far, i + nums[i]). O(n), O(1). Taking the largest jump can land on a 0 that a shorter jump would have skipped. Zeros are fine as long as you can jump over them.

questions.prompt: Given positive integers, return whether they can be split into two subsets with equal sums.
options: Subset-sum DP towards total / 2 (an odd total is an immediate no)
Sort and split at the middle index
Greedily add each number to the smaller side
Yes whenever the total is even
questions.explanation: Solve: target = total / 2; can = BooleanArray(target + 1), can[0] = true; for each x, for s from target down to x: can[s] = can[s] || can[s − x]. Answer can[target]. Greedy fails on [3, 3, 2, 2, 2]: the sides go 3 | 3, 5 | 3, 5 | 5, 7 | 5 — no split — yet 3 + 3 = 2 + 2 + 2.

questions.prompt: Return the length of the longest palindromic subsequence (not substring) of "bbbab".
options: 4 — dp[i][j] = dp[i + 1][j − 1] + 2 when s[i] = s[j], else max(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i][j − 1])
3 — expanding around each centre
5 — the length of the string
2 — the number of distinct letters
questions.explanation: Solve: "bbbb" (skipping the 'a') has length 4. A subsequence may skip characters, so expanding around centres — which finds the substring "bbb" — answers a different question. Fill the table by increasing length: O(n²).

questions.prompt: candidates = [2, 3, 6, 7], target = 7, each candidate reusable. Return every combination that sums to the target, with no duplicates.
options: Backtrack from a start index that never moves backwards — [[2, 2, 3], [7]]
List every ordering too — [[2, 2, 3], [2, 3, 2], [3, 2, 2], [7]]
Greedily take the largest first — [[7]]
Pairs only — []
questions.explanation: Solve: dfs(start, remaining, path): remaining == 0 → record; for i from start: if c[i] ≤ remaining, add it, dfs(i, remaining − c[i]) — i, not i + 1, allows reuse — then remove it. Never going back to an earlier index is what stops [2, 3, 2] appearing as a second copy of [2, 2, 3].

questions.prompt: Return every well-formed string of n = 3 pairs of parentheses.
options: Backtrack: add '(' while open < n, and ')' while close < open — 5 strings
Generate all 2^(2n) strings with no filtering — 64 strings
Place the pairs side by side — "()()()" only
Nest all the pairs — "((()))" only
questions.explanation: Solve: the two rules only allow valid prefixes, so every leaf is a valid answer: ((())), (()()), (())(), ()(()), ()()(). The count is the Catalan number C₃ = 5. Generating all 64 and filtering works but wastes most of the work.

questions.prompt: Given a grid of letters and a word, return whether the word can be traced through adjacent cells, using each cell at most once.
options: DFS from every cell matching the first letter, marking the path and un-marking on return
BFS that allows revisiting cells
Check that the grid has enough of each letter
Search each row as a plain string
questions.explanation: Solve: dfs(r, c, k): out of bounds or grid[r][c] != word[k] → false; k == last → true; mark grid[r][c] = '#', try the 4 neighbours with k + 1, then restore the letter. Un-marking is what lets another path use the cell later. Letter counts are necessary, not sufficient.

questions.prompt: Regular expression matching with '.' (any one character) and '*' (zero or more of the preceding one). Does "aab" match "c*a*b"?
options: Yes — 2-D DP where 'x*' either matches nothing (dp[i][j − 2]) or eats one matching character (dp[i − 1][j])
No — greedy matching lets 'c*' fail on 'a'
No — the pattern and the string have different lengths
Yes — delete every '*' and compare
questions.explanation: Solve: dp[i][j] = does s[0..i) match p[0..j). 'c*' matches zero c's, 'a*' matches "aa", 'b' matches 'b' → true. Deleting the stars gives "cab", which does not equal "aab"; greedy matching goes wrong on inputs like "aaa" against "a*a".

questions.prompt: Given a grid of non-negative costs, return the cheapest path from the top-left to the bottom-right moving only right or down.
options: cost[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(cost from above, cost from the left)
Greedy: always step to the cheaper neighbour
Dijkstra is required
Add up the main diagonal
questions.explanation: Solve: with only right and down moves the grid is a DAG, so one row-by-row pass settles every cell — O(m·n). Greedy can walk into an expensive corner. Dijkstra works too, but it is only needed when moves can go in every direction.

questions.prompt: Return the fewest cuts needed to split "abaab" into palindromes.
options: 1 — cuts[i] = min over palindromic s[j..i] of cuts[j − 1] + 1, with a precomputed isPalindrome table
2 — greedily take the longest palindromic prefix each time
3 — the number of distinct letters
4 — n − 1 cuts
questions.explanation: Solve: "a | baab" needs one cut. Greedy grabs the prefix "aba" first, leaving "ab", which needs two more pieces — 2 cuts. Precomputing isPalindrome[j][i] in O(n²) keeps the whole DP at O(n²).

quiz.title: Coding Round: Hard Classics
quiz.description: Rain water, histograms, two-array medians and the rest of the hard list.

questions.prompt: Given bar heights [0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1], return how much rain water they trap.
options: 6 — two pointers: move the lower side inward, adding its side's running max minus its height
22 — every bar filled up to the tallest bar
4 — the number of zero-height bars
3 — the height of the tallest bar
questions.explanation: Solve: water at i = min(maxLeft, maxRight) − height[i]. With l and r pointers, the side with the smaller max is limited by its own max, so add that and move it inward. O(n), O(1). Filling everything to the global maximum ignores the lower wall on each side.

questions.prompt: Return the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3].
options: 10 — a monotonic increasing stack; each popped bar extends between its smaller neighbours
36 — the tallest bar times the number of bars
6 — the shortest bar times the number of bars
11 — the two tallest bars added together
questions.explanation: Solve: push indices while heights rise. When a lower bar arrives, pop: the popped bar's rectangle spans from the new stack top + 1 to i − 1. The bars 5 and 6 give 5 × 2 = 10. Add a height-0 sentinel at the end to flush the stack. O(n).

questions.prompt: Return the median of two sorted arrays of sizes m and n in O(log(min(m, n))).
options: Binary search a cut in the smaller array so the two left sides together hold half of all elements
Merge the arrays and take the middle
Average the two arrays' own medians
Binary search the larger array's values only
questions.explanation: Solve: cut A at i and B at j = (m + n + 1) / 2 − i. The cut is right when A[i − 1] ≤ B[j] and B[j − 1] ≤ A[i]; otherwise move i. The median then comes from the max of the left sides and the min of the right sides. Merging is correct but O(m + n); averaging medians is simply wrong.

questions.prompt: Return the length of the longest valid (well-formed) parentheses substring in "()(()".
options: 2 — a stack of indices seeded with −1; on ')' pop, then length = i − the new top
4 — twice the number of matched pairs
5 — the length of the string
3 — the longest run of '('
questions.explanation: Solve: '(' pushes its index. ')' pops; if the stack is now empty, push i as the new base, else best = max(best, i − top). For "()(()" the unmatched '(' at index 2 splits the valid parts into "()" and "()", so the answer is 2. Counting pairs gives 4 because it ignores that split.

questions.prompt: nums has n + 1 values in 1..n, with one value repeated (possibly many times). Find it without modifying nums, in O(1) space.
options: Floyd's cycle detection over the links i → nums[i]
Sort the array and scan for neighbours
Put every value in a hash set
Actual sum minus n(n + 1) / 2
questions.explanation: Solve: treat each value as a next pointer. The repeated value has two incoming links, so it is where a cycle starts. Run slow/fast until they meet, then reset one to index 0 and step both once at a time — they meet at the duplicate. Sorting modifies the input, the set is O(n) space, and the sum trick fails once the value repeats more than twice.

questions.prompt: Return the smallest positive integer missing from an unsorted array, in O(n) time and O(1) space.
options: Cyclic sort: move each value v in 1..n to index v − 1, then return the first index whose value is wrong
Sort, then scan
Put the values in a hash set, then count up from 1
Return the maximum plus one
questions.explanation: Solve: while nums[i] in 1..n and nums[nums[i] − 1] != nums[i], swap it into place. Then the first i with nums[i] != i + 1 gives i + 1; if none, n + 1. Each swap places one value for good, so the total is O(n). Sorting is O(n log n) and the set is O(n) space.

questions.prompt: For each element, return how many smaller elements appear to its right. n = 10⁵.
options: Merge sort that counts how many right-half elements move ahead of each left-half element — O(n log n)
Nested loops
Sort the array and use each value's sorted index
A monotonic stack
questions.explanation: Solve: sort (value, originalIndex) pairs with merge sort. While merging, when a left element is placed, add the number of right elements already placed before it to count[originalIndex]. A Fenwick tree over value ranks, scanned right to left, also works. Nested loops are 10¹⁰ operations.

questions.prompt: Given a binary matrix, return the area of the largest square containing only 1s.
options: side[r][c] = 1 + min(above, left, above-left) when the cell is 1; the answer is the max side²
Count all the 1s and take the square root
The longest row of 1s, squared
BFS from every 1
questions.explanation: Solve: a square ending at (r, c) can only be as large as the smallest of the three squares it builds on, plus one. One pass, O(m·n), and a single row of memory is enough. Counting 1s ignores whether they are next to each other.

questions.prompt: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing path in a matrix, moving up, down, left or right.
options: DFS with a memo per cell — increasing moves form a DAG, so each cell is solved once: O(m·n)
BFS from every cell with no memo
Sort the cells and take the longest sorted row
Dijkstra with negated values
questions.explanation: Solve: len(r, c) = 1 + max(len(neighbour)) over neighbours with a larger value, cached. Strictly increasing moves can never loop, so memoised DFS is safe — no visited set needed. Without the memo the same paths are re-explored exponentially.

questions.prompt: Given intervals, return the fewest you must remove so the rest do not overlap.
options: Sort by end; keep an interval if it starts at or after the last kept end — answer = n − kept
Sort by length and drop the longest first
Remove every interval that overlaps anything
Sort by start and keep the first interval of each overlap
questions.explanation: Solve: the earliest-ending interval leaves the most room for the rest (exchange argument), so keeping greedily by end time maximises how many stay. Dropping the longest first fails when one short interval overlaps two others that do not overlap each other.

quiz.title: Picture Round: Solve the Diagram
quiz.description: Harder whiteboard problems — weighted graphs, DP tables, heaps and windows drawn out for you to solve.

questions.prompt: Edge labels are travel costs. What is the cheapest path from A to E?
options: 7, via A–C–B–D–E
8, via A–B–D–E
9, via A–C–D–E
6, via A–C–D–E
questions.explanation: Solve with Dijkstra: settle A = 0. C = 1 is closest; through C, B improves from 4 to 3 and D becomes 6. Settle B = 3; through B, D improves to 4. Settle D = 4, so E = 7. The direct A–B edge looks shorter but costs more than going round through C.

questions.prompt: Arrows point from a task to the task that depends on it. Which order runs every task after its prerequisites?
options: B, A, E, C, D
A, C, B, E, D
B, E, D, A, C
D, C, E, A, B
questions.explanation: Solve: check each arrow. A→C, B→C, C→D, B→E, E→D. In B, A, E, C, D, every task comes before everything it points to. A, C, B… runs C before its prerequisite B; B, E, D… runs D before C. Kahn's algorithm builds such an order by repeatedly taking a task with no remaining prerequisites.

questions.prompt: These are today's meetings. What is the fewest meeting rooms that fits them all?
questions.explanation: Solve: the answer is the most meetings running at one moment. From 15 to 20, the 0–30, 10–25 and 15–20 meetings all overlap, so you need 3 rooms. At 10, the 5–10 meeting ends just as 10–25 starts, and a room freed at 10 can be reused at 10. Sweep the start/end events in time order, or keep a min-heap of end times.

questions.prompt: Move only right or down, adding each cell's cost. What is the cheapest total from the top-left to the bottom-right?
options: 7 — right, right, down, down
9 — always step to the cheaper neighbour
8 — down, right, right, down
5 — the three corner cells
questions.explanation: Solve: best[r][c] = cost + min(best above, best left). Row 1: 1, 4, 5. Row 2: 2, 7, 6. Row 3: 6, 8, 7. The answer is 7: 1 → 3 → 1 → 1 → 1. Greedy steps down to the cheap 1 first, then gets stuck paying 4 and 2 — a total of 9.

questions.prompt: Is this a valid binary search tree?
options: No — 6 is in 10's right subtree but smaller than 10
Yes — every node is ordered correctly against its own children
No — 20 is too large for a BST
Yes — its in-order traversal is sorted
questions.explanation: Solve: every node in the right subtree must be greater than the root, not just greater than its parent. 6 < 15 is fine locally, but 6 < 10 breaks the rule. Pass bounds down: the right subtree of 10 has range (10, ∞), and 6 falls outside it. The in-order walk 5, 10, 6, 15, 20 is not sorted either.

questions.prompt: Edges are added in the order e1 to e5, using union-find. Which edge is the first to join two nodes that are already connected (a cycle)?
options: e4 (A–D)
e3 (B–C)
e5 (C–E)
None — the edges form a tree
questions.explanation: Solve: e1 unions {A, B}; e2 unions {C, D}; e3 joins them into {A, B, C, D}. At e4, find(A) == find(D) — already one set — so A–D closes the loop A–B–C–D–A. e5 then adds E safely. This is exactly how Kruskal decides which edges to skip.

questions.prompt: For each element, find the next element to its right that is strictly greater (−1 if there is none). What is the output?
questions.explanation: Solve: keep a stack of indices whose answer is still unknown. The 1 arrives, is not bigger than 2, and gets pushed. The second 2 pops the 1 (answer 2) but not the first 2, because it is not strictly greater. Then 4 pops both 2s (answer 4). 3 is smaller than 4, and nothing follows, so 4 and 3 get −1. Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n).

questions.prompt: Longest substring without repeating characters: the window holds "abc", and R reaches another 'a'. Where does the left edge move?
options: To index 1 — just past the earlier 'a'
To index 3 — restart at R
It stays at 0 — the window just grows
To index 2 — halfway through the window
questions.explanation: Solve: keep lastSeen[ch]. On a repeat, L = max(L, lastSeen[ch] + 1) — here 0 + 1 = 1 — so the window becomes "bca" with no repeat. Restarting at R throws away "bc", which is still valid. The max() stops L moving backwards when the old copy is already outside the window. The answer for "abcabcbb" is 3.

questions.prompt: Can this graph's nodes be coloured with two colours so that no edge joins two nodes of the same colour?
options: No — it is a cycle of odd length (5)
Yes — every node has exactly two neighbours
No — any graph with a cycle fails
Yes — 5 nodes can always be split into two groups
questions.explanation: Solve: colour A red; B and E must be blue; C must be red and D blue — but D and E are neighbours and both blue. Any odd cycle forces this clash, and a graph is two-colourable exactly when it has no odd cycle. A square (an even cycle) would be fine, so "has a cycle" is the wrong reason.

questions.prompt: A running median uses two heaps, shown here. After inserting 6 and rebalancing, what is the median?
questions.explanation: Solve: 6 > 5 (the low half's top), so it goes into the high half: low {5, 3, 1}, high {6, 7, 9}. The sizes are equal (3 and 3), so no rebalance is needed, and the median is the average of the two tops: (5 + 6) / 2 = 5.5. Sorted, that is 1, 3, 5 | 6, 7, 9.

quiz.description: An outage, an error spike and a new cache — one engineer's night, with questions on each part.

questions.prompt: Which services are broken because the database is down?
options: Gate, Auth and Cat — everything with a path to DB
Only Auth and Cat — the services that call DB directly
Every service
Gate, Auth, Cat and Play
questions.explanation: Solve: reverse the arrows and BFS from DB. DB's callers are Auth and Cat; their caller is Gate. Play only needs Cache, which is healthy, so videos that are already cached keep playing. Stopping at direct callers misses Gate, which fails because Auth and Cat do.

questions.prompt: After the fix, services restart one at a time, each only once everything it needs is up. Which order works?
options: DB, Cache, Auth, Cat, Play, Gate
Gate, Auth, Cat, DB, Cache, Play
DB, Auth, Gate, Cache, Cat, Play
Cache, Play, Cat, DB, Auth, Gate
questions.explanation: Solve: this is a topological order of the reversed graph — dependencies first. Check each arrow: Auth and Cat after DB, Cat and Play after Cache, Gate after Auth and Cat. DB, Auth, Gate… starts Gate before Cat is up; Cache, Play, Cat… starts Cat before DB.

story.title: StreamFlix · The 3 a.m. page
story.text: Rahim is on call at StreamFlix, a video-streaming service. At 3 a.m. the database (DB) goes down. The diagram shows which service needs which: Gate is the API gateway, Cat the catalog, Play the video player. An arrow from A to B means A needs B to work.

questions.prompt: A teammate proposes that DB should call Gate to report its health. What does that do to the restart plan?
options: It creates a cycle Gate → Auth → DB → Gate, so no valid restart order exists
Nothing — it is just one more arrow
DB now simply has to start last
Gate can now start without Auth
questions.explanation: Solve: every service on the loop now needs another service on the loop to be up first, so none of them can start first — there is no topological order. Find it with DFS: reaching a node still on the current path means a cycle. The usual fix is to make the health report asynchronous, so DB does not need Gate.

questions.prompt: What is the most errors in any 3 consecutive minutes?
options: 119 — the three worst minutes
questions.explanation: Solve: slide a 3-minute window, adding the minute that enters and subtracting the one that leaves. The sums are 45, 81, 83, 84, 48 — the best is 38 + 5 + 41 = 84. The three worst minutes (41, 40, 38) add up to 119, but they are not consecutive.

story.title: StreamFlix · The error spike
story.text: While the database recovers, Rahim watches the errors-per-minute dashboard. Before writing the incident report, he has a few questions about the numbers.

questions.prompt: For the report, what is the median number of errors per minute across these 7 minutes?
options: 18.7 — the average
questions.explanation: Solve: sorted, the minutes are 2, 2, 3, 5, 38, 40, 41; the middle (4th) value is 5. The average is 131 / 7 ≈ 18.7, pulled up by the three spike minutes — which is why incident reports quote the median for a "typical" minute. Quickselect finds it in O(n) average without sorting.

story.title: StreamFlix · The error spike
story.text: While the database recovers, Rahim watches the errors-per-minute dashboard. Before writing the incident report, he has a few questions about the numbers.

questions.prompt: A known bug produces exactly 79 errors split across two minutes. Do any two minutes add up to 79, and how do you check in one pass?
options: Yes — 38 and 41; keep a set of values seen so far and look up 79 − x
No — no two minutes add up to 79
Yes — 40 and 38
Yes — 40 and 41
questions.explanation: Solve: walk the minutes; for each x, check whether 79 − x is in the seen set, then add x. At 41 the set already holds 38, so 38 + 41 = 79. 40 + 38 = 78 and 40 + 41 = 81 are close but wrong. O(n) time — the Two Sum pattern.

story.title: StreamFlix · The error spike
story.text: While the database recovers, Rahim watches the errors-per-minute dashboard. Before writing the incident report, he has a few questions about the numbers.

questions.prompt: A viewer requests video A, then a new video D. Which video gets evicted?
options: B
A — it was at the bottom
C
D — the newest one is dropped
questions.explanation: Solve: requesting A is a hit, so A moves to the top: A, C, B. D is a miss and the cache is full, so the least recently used video — now B at the bottom — is evicted. A was at the bottom a moment ago, but using it made it the most recent.

questions.prompt: After those two requests (A, then D), what does the cache hold, most recent first?
options: D, A, C
D, C, B
A, D, C
D, B, C
questions.explanation: Solve: C, B, A → request A → A, C, B → add D, evict B → D, A, C. Each access moves its item to the front, and eviction always takes the item at the back.

story.title: StreamFlix · The cache
story.text: To take load off the database, Rahim adds a cache that holds 3 videos and evicts the least recently used one when it is full. The figure shows the cache right now, most recently used on top.

questions.prompt: From that state (D, A, C), the next requests are C, E, A. How many of those three are cache hits?
options: 1 — C hits; A was evicted just before it came back
2 — C and A both hit
questions.explanation: Solve: C hits → C, D, A. E misses and evicts A → E, C, D. A misses → A, E, C. Only one hit. A was in the cache two requests earlier, but E pushed it out — this is how a cache that is too small thrashes.

questions.prompt: Traffic grows, and 3 slots are far too few. Rahim measures hit rates: 10 slots → 60%, 100 → 90%, 1,000 → 92%. Which size should he choose?
options: About 100 — beyond that, 10× more memory buys only 2 more points
1,000 — always take the highest hit rate
10 — the smallest cache is cheapest
It cannot be decided without doubling to 2,000
questions.explanation: Solve: going from 10 to 100 slots cuts DB traffic from 40% to 10% of requests — four times less load. Going from 100 to 1,000 only cuts it from 10% to 8%, for ten times the memory. Popularity is skewed (a few videos get most views), so returns flatten quickly; pick the knee of the curve and say why.
